They thereby may cease to be Sanatanis, but cannot cease to be Hindus. Sikhs are Hindus in the sense of our definition of Hindutva and not in any religious sense whatever. Religiously they are Sikhs as Jains are Jains, Lingayats are Lingayats, Vaishnavas are Vaishnavas; but all of us racially and nationally and culturally are a polity and a people, one and indivisible, most fitly and from times immemorial called Hindus. No other word can express our racial oneness—not even Bharatiya can do that for reasons dealt with in the forgoing pages. Bharatiya indicates an Indian and expresses a larger generalization but cannot express racial unity of us Hindus. We are Sikhs, and Hindus and Bharatiyas. We are all three put together and none exclusively.

Another reason besides this fear of being indentified with the followers of Sanatanpanth which added to the zeal of some of our Sikh brothers and made them insist on getting classed separately as non-Hindus, was a political one. This is not the place of entering into merits or demerits of special representation. The Sikhs were naturally anxious to guard the special interests of their community and if the Mohammedans could enjoy the privilege of a special and communal .representation, we do not understand why any other important minority in India should not claim similar concession. But we feel that, that claim should not have been backed up by our Sikh brothers by an untenable and suicidal plea of being non-Hindus. Sikhs, to guard their own interests could have pressed for and succeeded in securing special and communal representation on the ground of being an important minority as our non-Brahmins and other communities have done without renouncing their birthright of Hindutva. Our Sikh brotherhood is certainly not a less important community than the Mohammedans —in fact to us Hindus they are more important than any non-Hindu community in India. The harm that a special and communal representation does is never so great as the har done by the attitude of racial aloofness. Let the Sikhs, the Jains, the Lingayats, the non-Brahmins and even, for the matter of that. Brahmins press and fight for the right of special and communal representation, if they honestly look upon it as indispensable for their communal growth. For their growth is the growth of the whole Hindu-society. Even in ancient times our four main castes enjoyed a kind of special representation on communal basis in our councils of State as well as in local bodies. They could do that without refusing to get fused into the larger whole and incorporated into the wider generalization of Hindutva, Let the Sikhs be classed as Sikhs religiously, but as Hindus racially and culturally.

The brave people placed their heads by hundreds under the executioner's axe rather than disown their Guru. Will they disown their seed, forswear their fathers and sell their birthright for a mess of pottage ? God forbid! Let our minorities remember that if strength lies in union, then in Hindutva lies the firmest and yet the dearest bond that can effect a real, lasting and powerful union of our people. You may fancy that it pays you to remain aloof for the passing hour, but it would do incalculable harm to this our ancient race and civilization as a whole —and especially to yourselves. Your interests are indissolubly bound with the interests of your other Hindu brethren. Whenever in the future as in the past a foreigner raises a sword against the Hindu civilization it is sure to strike you as deadly as any other Hindu community. Whenever in future as in the past the Hindus as a people come to their own and under a Shivaji or a Ranjit, a Ramchandra or a Dharma, an Ashoka or an Amoghwarsha feeling the quickening touch of life and activity mount the pinnacles of glory and greatness—that day would shed its lustre on you as well as on any other members of our Hindu commonwealth. So, brothers, be not lured by the immediate gains, partly or otherwise, nor be duped by misreadings and misinterpretations of history. I was once told by one who posing as a Granthi was nevertheless convicted for committing a dacoity in the house of a Brahmin to whom he owed money and whom he consequently murdered, that the Sikhs were not Hindus and that they could incur no guilt by killing a Brahmin as the sons of Govindsing were betrayed by a Brahmin cook. Fortunately there was another Sikh gentleman and a real Granthi and was recognized as such by all learned Sikhs who immediately contradicted and cornered him by several

examples of Matidas and others, who had sheltered the Guru and proved true to the Sikhs even unto martyrdom. Was not Shivaji betrayed by his kith and kin and his grandson again by a Pisal who too was a Hindu ? But did Shivaji or his nation disown their race and cease to be Hindus? Many of the Sikhs have acted treacherously first at the time of desertion of the heroic Banda, then again at the time of the last war of the Khalsa forces with the English. Guru Govindsing himself was deserted by a number of Sikhs in the very thick of the fight and it was this act of treacherous cowardice of these Sikhs which by forcing our lion-hearted Guru to try a desperate sortie gave occasion to that cursed Brahmin wretch to betray his two sons. If, therefore, for the crime of the latter we cease to be Hindus, then for the crime of the former we ought to cease to be Sikhs too !

This minority of the Hindus as well as the major communities of them did not fall from the skies as separate creations. They are an organic growth that has its roots embedded deep in a common land and in a common culture. You cannot pick up a lamb and by tying a Kachchha and Kripan on it, make a lion of it! If the Guru succeeded in forming a band of martyrs and warriors he could do so because the race that produced him as well as that band was capable of being moulded thus. The lion's seed alone can breed lions. The flower cannot say 'I bloom and smell: surely I came out of the stalk alone — I have nothing to do with the roots!' No more can we deny our seed or our blood. As soon as you point at a Sikh who was true to his Guru you have automatically pointed at a Hindu who was true to the Guru for before being a Sikh he was, and yet continues to be a Hindu. So long as our Sikh brethren are true to Sikhism they must of necessity continue to be Hindus for so long must this land, this Bharatbhumika from Sindhu to the seas, remain their Fatherland and their Holyland. It is by ceasing to be Sikhs alone that they may, perhaps, cease to be Hindus. We have dealt at some length with this special case of our Sikh brotherhood as all those arguments and remarks would automatically test all similar cases of our other non- Vaidik sects and religions in the light of our definition. The Devsamajis for example are agnostics but Hindutva has little to do with agnosticism, or for the matter of that, atheism. The Devsamajis look on this land as the land of their forefathers, their fatherland as well as their Holyland and are therefore Hindus. Of course, it is superfluous, after all this to refer to our Aryasamaj. All the essentials of Hindutva hold good in their case so eminently that they are Hindus. We, in fact, are unable to hit upon any case that can lay our definition open to the charge of exclusiveness.

In one case alone it seems to offer some real difficulty. Is, for example. Sister Nivedita a Hindu ? If ever an exception proves the rule it does so here. Our patriotic and noble- minded sister had adopted our land from Sindu to the seas as her Fatherland. She truly loved it as such, and had our nation been free, we would have been the first to bestow the right of citizenship on such loving souls. So the first essential may, to some extent, be said to hold good in her case. The second essential of common blood of Hindu parentage must, nevertheless and necessarily, be absent in such cases as these. The sacrament of marriage with a Hindu which really fuses and is universally admitted to do so, two beings into one may be said to remove this disqualification. But although this second essential failed, either way to hold good in her case, the third important qualification of Hindutva did entitle her to be recognized as a Hindu. For she had adopted our culture and come to

adore our land as her Holyland. She felt, she was a Hindu and that is, apart from all technicalities, the real and the most important test. But we must not forget that we have to determine the essentials of Hindutva in the sense in which the word is actually used by an overwhelming majority of people. And therefore we must say that any convert of non- Hindu parentage to Hindutva can be a Hindu, if bona fide, he or she adopts our land as his or her country and marries a Hindu, thus coming to love our land as a real Fatherland, and adopts our culture and thus adores our land as the Punyabhu. The children of such a union as that would, other things being equal, be most emphatically Hindus. We are not authorized to go further.

But by coming to believe into the tenets of any sects of the Hindus a foreign convert may be recognized as a Sanatani, or a Sikh, or a Jain; and as these religions being founded by or revealed to Hindus, go by he name of Hindudharma the convert too, may be religiously called a Hindu. But it must be understood that a religious or cultural convert possesses only one of the three essentials of Hindutva and it is owing to this disqualification that people generally do not recognise as a Hindu any one and every one who subscribes to the religious beliefs of our race. So deep our feeling of gratitude is towards a Sister Nivedita or an Annie Besant for the services they rendered to the cause of our Motherland and our culture, so soft-hearted and sensitive to the touch of love as a race we Hindus are, that Sister Nivedita or a person like her who so completely identifies his or her being with the Being of our people, is almost unconsciously received in the Hindu fold. But it should be done as an exception to the rule. The rule itself must neither be too rigid nor too elastic The several tests to which we have subjected our definition of Hindutva have, we believe, proved that it satisfies both these requirements and involves neither Avyapti nor Ativyapti; neither contraction nor expansion of the exact connotation.

docs.title: Unique Natural Blessings to Hindusthan
docs.text:
So far we have not allowed any considerations of utility to prejudice our inquiry. But having come to its end it will not be out of place to see how far the attributes, which we found to be the essentials of Hindutva, contribute towards the strength, cohesion, and progress of our people. Do these essentials constitute a foundation so broad, so deep, so strong that basing upon it the Hindu people can build a future which can face and repel the attacks of all the adverse winds that blow; or does the Hindu race stand on feet of clay ?

Some of the ancient nations raised huge walls so as to convert a whole country into a fortified castle. To-day their walls are trodden to dust or are but scarcely discernible by a few scattered mounds here and there; while the people they were meant to protect are not discernible at all. Our ancient neighbours, the Chinese, laboured from generation to generation and raised a rampart, embracing the limits of an empire, so wide, so high, so strong, a wonder of the human world. That too, as all human wonders must, sank under its own weight. But behold the ramparts of Nature! Have they not, these Himalayas, been standing there as one whose desires are satisfied—so they seemed to the Vedic bard —so they seem to us to-day. These are our ramparts that have converted this vast continent into a cosy castle.

You take up buckets and fill your trenches with water and call it a moat. Behold, Varuna himself, with his one hand pushing continents aside, fills the gap by pouring seas on seas with the other ! This Indian ocean with its bays and gulfs, is our moat.

These are our frontier lines bringing within our reach the advantages of an island as well as an insular country.

She is the richly endowed, daughter of God—this our Motherland. Her rivers are deep and perennial. Her land is yielding to plough and her fields loaded with golden harvests. Her necessaries of life are few and a genial nature yields them all almost for the asking. Rich in her fauna, rich in her flora, she knows she owes it all to the immediate source of light and heat—the sun. She covets not the icy lands; blessed be they and their frozen latitudes. If heat is at times ' enervating' here, cold is at times benumbing there. If cold induces manual labour, heat removes much of its very necessity. She takes more delight in quenched thirst than in the parched throat. Those who have not, let them delight in exerting to have. But those who have—may be allowed to derive pleasure from the very fact of having. Father Thames is free to work at feverish speed, wrapped in his icy sheets. She loves to visit her ghats and watch her boats gliding down the Ganges on her moonlit waters. With the plough, the peacocks, and lotus, the elephant and the Gita, she is willing to forego, if that must be, whatever advantage the colder latitudes enjoy. She knows she cannot have all her own way. Her gardens are green and shady, her granaries well- stocked, her waters crystal, her flowers scented, her fruits juicy and her herbs healing. Her brush is dipped in the colours of Dawn and her flute resonant with the music of Gokul. Verily Hind is the richly endowed daugher of God.

Neither the English nor the French with the exception of the Chinese and perhaps the Americans, no people are gifted with a land that can equal in natural strength and richness the land of Sindusthan. A country, a common home is the first important essential of a stable strong nationality; and as of all countries in the world our country can hardly be surpassed by any in its capacity to afford a soil so specially fitted for the growth of a great nation; we Hindus whose very first article of faith is the love we bear to the common Fatherland, have in that love the strongest talismanic tie that can bind close and keep a nation firm and enthuse and enable it to accomplish things greater than ever.

The second essential of Hindutva puts the estimate of our latent powers of national cohesion and greatness yet higher. No country in the world with the exception of China again, is peopled by a race so homogeneous, yet so ancient and yet so strong both numerically and vitally. The Americans too, whom we found equally fortunate with us so far as excellent geographical basis of nationality is concerned, are decidedly left behind. Mohammedans are no race nor are the Christians. They are a religious unit, yet neither a racial nor a national one. But we Hindus, if possible, are all the three put together, and live under our ancient and common roof. The numerical strength of our race is an asset that cannot be too highly prized.

And culture ? The English and the Americans feel they are kith and kin because they possess a Shakespeare in common. But not only Kalidas or a Bhasa but, Oh Hindus ! ye

possess a Ramayan and Mahabharat in common—and the Vedas ! One of the national songs the American children are taught to sing attempts to rouse their sense of eternal self-importance by pointing out to the hundred years twice told that stand behind their history. The Hindu counts his years not by centuries but by cycles—the Yuga and the Kalpa and amazed asks

The Uttra Kosala of Raghupathi is nowhere to be seen, nor is Shri Krishna's city of Mathura.

He does not attempt to rouse the sense of self-importance so much as the sense of proportion which is Truth. And that has perhaps made him last longer than Ramses and Nebuchadnezzar. If a people that had no past has no future, then a people that had produced an unending galaxy of heroes and hero-worshippers and who are conscious of having fought with and vaquished the forces whose might struck Greece and Rome, the Pharaohs and the Incas, dead, have in their history a guarantee of their future greatness more assuring than any other people on earth yet possess.

But besides culture the tie of common holyland has at times proved stronger than the chains of a Motherland. Look at the Mohammedans. Mecca to them is a sterner reality than Delhi or Agra. Some of I them do not make any secret of being bound to sacrifice all India if that be to the glory of Islam or could save the city of their prophet. Look at the Jews; neither centuries of prosperity nor sense of gratitude for the shelter they found, can make them more attached or even equally attached to the several countries they inhabit. Their love is, and must necessarily be divided between the land of their birth and the land of their Prophets. If the Zionists' dreams are ever realized—if Palestine becomes a Jewish State and it will gladden us almost as much as our Jewish friends—they, like the Mohammedans would naturally set the interests of their Holyland above those of their Motherland in America and Europe and in case of war between their adopted country and the Jewish State, would naturally sympathise with the latter, if indeed they do not bodily go over to it. History is too full of examples of such desertions to cite particulars. The crusades again, attest to the wonderful influence that a common holyland exercises over peoples widely separated in race, nationality and language, to bind and hold them together.

The ideal conditions, therefore, under which a nation can attain perfect solidarity and cohesion would, other things being equal, be found in the case of those people who inhabit the land they adore, the land of whose forefathers is also the land of their Gods and Angels, of Seers and Prophets; the scenes of whose history are also the scenes of their mythology. The Hindus are about the only people who are blessed with these ideal conditions that are at the same time incentive to national solidarity, cohesion and greatness. Not even the Chinese are blessed thus. Only Arabia and Palestine, if ever the Jews can succeed in founding their state there, can be said to possess this unique advantage. But Arabia is incomparably poorer in the natural, cultural, historical, and numerical essentials of a great people; and even if the dreams of the Zionists are ever realized into a Palestine State still they too must be equally lacking in these.

England, France, Germany, Italy, Turkey proper, Persia, Japan, Afganistan, Egypt of to-day (for the old descendants of 'Punto' and their Egypt is dead long since), and other African states, Mexico, Peru, Chile (not to mention states and nations lesser than all these ), though racially more or less hemogeneous are yet less advantageously situated than we are in geographical, cultural, historical and numerical essentials, besides lacking the unique gift of a sanctified Motherland. Of the remaining nations, Russia in Europe, and United states in America, though geographically equally well-gifted with us, are yet poorer, in almost every other requisite of nationality. China alone of the present comity of nations is almost as richly gifted with the geographical, racial, cultural essentials as the Hindus are. Only in the possession of a common, a sacred and a perfect language, the Sanskrit, and a sanctified Motherland, we are so far as the essentials that contribute to national solidarity are concerned more fortunate.

Thus the actual essentials of Hindutva are, as this running sketch reveals, also the ideal essentials of nationality. If we would, we could build on this foundation of Hindutva a future greater than what any other people on earth can dream of, greater even than our own past; provided we are able to utilize our opportunities. For let our people remember that great combinations are the order of the day. The league of Nations, the alliances of powers Pan-Islamism, Pan-Slavism, Pan-Ethiopism, all little beings are seeking to get themselves incorporated into greater wholes, so as to be better-fitted for the struggle for existence and power. Those who are not naturally and historically blessed with numerical or geographical or racial advantages are seeking to share them with others. Woe to those who have them already as their birth-right and know them not; or worse, despise them! The nations of the world are desperately trying to find a place in this or that combination for aggression—can any one of you, Oh Hindus! whether Jain or Samaji or Sanatani or Sikh or any other subsection afford to cut yourselves off or fall out and destroy the ancient, the natural and the organic combination that already exists?—a combination that is bound not by any scraps of paper nor by the ties of exigencies alone, but by the ties of blood, birth and culture? Strengthen them if you can: pull down the barriers that have survived their utility, of castes and customs, of sects and sections: What of interdining?— but intermarriages between provinces and provinces, castes and castes, be encouraged where they do not exist. But where they already exist as between the Sikhs and Sanatanies, Jains and Vaishnayas, Lingayats and Non-Lingayats-suicideal be the hand that tries to cut the nuptial tie. Let the minorities remember they would be cutting the very branch on which they stand. Strenghten every tie that binds you to the main organism, whether of blood or language or common Motherland. Let this ancient and noble stream of Hindu blood flow from vein to vien, from Attock to Cuttack till at last the Hindu people get fused and welded into an indivisible whole, till our race gets consolidated and strong sharp as steel.

Just cast a glance at the past, then at the present : Pan-Islamism in Asia, the political Leagues in Europe, the Pan-Ethiopic movement in Africa and America- and then see, O Hindus, if your future is not entirely bound up with the future of India and the future of India is bound up in the last resort, with Hindu strength. We are trying our best, as we ought to do, to develop the consciousness of and a sense of attachment to the greater whole, whereby Hindus, Mohammedans, Parsis Christians, and Jews would feel as

Indians first and every other thing afterwards. But whatever progress India may have made to that goal one thing remains almost axiomatically true- not only in India but everywhere in the world-that a nation requires a foundation to stand upon and the essence of the life of a nation is the life of that portion of its citizens whose interests and history and aspirations are most closely bound up with the land and who thus provide the real foundation to the structure of their national state. Take the case of Turkey. The young Turks after the revolution had to open their Parliament and military institutions to Armenians and Christians on a non-religious and secular basis. But when the war with Servia came the Christians and Armenians first wavered and then many a regiment consisting of them went bodily over to the Servians, who politically and racially and religiously were more closely bound up with them. Take the case of America: when the German war broke out she suddenly had to face danger of desertions of her German citizens; while the Negro citizens there sympathise more with their brethren in Africa than with their white countrymen. American State, in the last resort, must stand or fall with the fortunes of its Anglo-Saxon constituents. So with the Hindus, they being the people, whose past,present and future are most closely bound with the soil of Hindusthan as Pitribhu, as Punyabhu, they constitute the foundation, the bedrock, the reserved forces of the Indian state. Therefore even from the point of Indian nationality, must ye, O Hindus, consolidate and strengthen Hindu nationality; not to give wanton offence to any of our non-Hindu compatriots, in fact to any one in the world but in just and urgent defence of our race and land; to render it impossible for others to betray her or to subject her to unprovoked attack by any of those 'Pan-isms' that are struggling forth from continent to continent. As long as other communities in India or in the world are not respectively planning India first or mankind first, but all are busy in organizing offensive and defensive alliances and combinations on entirely narrow racial or religious or national basis, so long, at least, so long O Hindus, strengthen if you can those subtle bonds that like nerve threads bind you in one organic social being. Those of you who in a fit suicidal try to cut off the most vital of those ties and dare to disown the name Hindu will find to their cost that in doing so they have cut themselves off from the very source of our racial life and strength.

The presence of only a few of these essentials of nationality which we have found to constitute Hindutva enabled little nations like Spain or Portugal to get themselves lionized in the world. But when all of those ideal conditions obtain here what is there in the human world that the Hindus cannot accomplish ?

Thirty crores of people, with India for their basis of operation, for their Fatherland and for their Holyland with such a history behind them, bound together by ties of a common blood and common culture can dictate their terms to the whole world. A day will come when mankind will have to face the force.

Equally certain it is that whenever the Hindus come to hold such a position whence they could dictate terms to the whole world — those terms cannot be very different from the terms which Gita dictates or the Buddha lays down. A Hindu is most intensely so, when he ceases to be Hindu; and with a Shankar claims the whole earth for a Benares ' Waranasi Medini !' or with a Tukaram exclaims

'my country! Oh brothers, 'the limits of the Universe — there the frontiers of my country lie ?'

docs.title: Scene 1
docs.text:
(The temple of the Goddess in the hermitage. Dancing girls sing a song.)

Song:

Song Details: Title: Kitī tari sulalit sahaj-gīti Rāga: Yaman | Tāla: Ektāl | Chāl: Hālā, Madhumatī Vilasit Original: किती तरि सुललित सहज- गीति- । तार न बहु ताणी ।। ध्रु. ।। ताणिशि तनु-बीन तुटे शिथिल तरी गीति नुठे, अति ते करित हानी ॥ १ ॥ Translation: How graceful and easy the melody – yet strain not the string too much, (Chorus) Shouldst thou strain the lute-string of the body, it snaps; should it be slack, the melody rises not, causing great harm.

(As the girls depart singing, Siddhartha Gautama and Kaunḍinya enter.)

Siddhartha: Kaunḍinya, that was the song! Didst thou hear it? This song which these dancers sang just now, I heard it once before. And thou wouldst be astonished, but this song of the dancers kindled a divine light in my heart, like unto a mystic mantra. And in that light, I could trace the path to nirvāṇa (liberation) through the deep darkness of this hermitage and reach the foot of the Bodhivṛkṣa (Bodhi Tree). It is well-known that we were engaged in severe self-mortification on the banks of the Nirañjanā river, to witness firsthand what truth lay in the path of tapas (asceticism), which declares that liberation is attained by torturing, tormenting, and destroying one's body and senses, offering them as a sacrifice. Kaunḍinya, is there any means to free this entire world from the four great sorrows: birth, death, old age, and sickness? With such a yearning, I vowed that—

Song:

Song Details: Title: Vimukta karu he Tāla: Tritāl | Chāl: Pītanake Original: विमुक्त करु हे । आर्त जगत । पासुनि जन्ममरणा ।। ध्रु. ।। साधन शोधाया । राज्य स्वजन अरे प्राणही । सोडीन लोक शोक हरणा ।। १ ।। Translation: This sorrowing world shall we free / From birth and death's decree. (Chorus) To seek the means / My kingdom, kin, yea, even life / Will I forsake, to end human grief.

Siddhartha: ...With such a resolute determination, I renounced this sorrowful worldly existence, abandoning my Śākya kingdom, my young wife Goddess Yaśodharā, my newborn son Rāhul – all my possessions – and came to dwell in this forest. Then, I observed many vows of fasting and austerity, even to eating but a single grain a day. Yet, enlightenment eluded me. Finally, I lay day and night, nigh unto death. But this only destroyed what little power of thought I had; how then could greater knowledge be attained? Just then, one day, the dancing girls passed by, singing this very song: ‘Do not loosen the string of the vīṇā (lute) too much; else no melody shall rise. Nor stretch it too taut, lest the vīṇā itself break.’ The same condition applies to the senses, this lute of the body. If these senses are excessively indulged, thou shalt miss the music of peace; if thou torturest them too much, thou shalt also forfeit the music of peace. But if thou nurturest these horses of the senses appropriately, yet holdest their reins like an expert charioteer, and makest use of them, then that state of equipoise shall render thy journey on the path of knowledge pleasant, and ultimately grant thee nirvāṇa. This principle convinced me, and I abandoned that self-mortification. I partook of food and, maintaining a balanced diet and conduct, was able to experience the supreme bliss of nirvāṇa through the path of contemplative knowledge under the shade of that Bodhivṛkṣa. Kaunḍinya, is the principle concerning the sacrificial path of violence likewise true for this path of self-mortifying tapas? Tell me, pray! What is the principle of the Tathāgata (one who has thus come/gone) Buddha regarding the sacrificial path of violence?

Kaunḍinya: O Bhagavan Buddha-deva, I have fully grasped thy principle regarding violent sacrifices. Plavā hyete adṛḍhāḥ yajñarūpāḥ (These forms of sacrifice are unstable boats). Gather heaps of cow dung and firewood, make a huge bonfire of it, and then, with solemn mantras, slice and dice the throats, hearts, fat, and sinews of innocent, frolicking lambs and calves, their legs bound, as one would cut vegetables; and then, with streams of blood, burn their various pieces of flesh in the fire, saying, ‘This is for Indra, this for the Maruts, this for Varuṇa!’ If deities are appeased by such bloody sacrifices, why should they not be appeased by a slaughterhouse? This is not ritual; this is butchery, and if gods are truly pleased by it, then they must be demons, not gods! They say that by slaying lambs and calves, man attains liberation! What madness is this! Moreover, even in the heaven attained by sacrifice, the tales of the gods themselves tell us that they too are not free from envy, wrath, fear, sorrow, and discontent. But, O Bhagavan, did those who devised the notion that liberation is attained and ancestral spirits are appeased by animal sacrifice, invent it solely to deceive the world?

Siddhartha: Nay. I do not say that they intentionally deceived the world. It was an honest error on their part. It was but a step in humanity's commendable efforts to discover the eternal and immortal fundamental principle of the world and to find a means to freedom from all suffering. It was an intellectual delusion. But once that illusion is dispelled by experience and reflection, what wise man would cling to it still? By self-mortifying tapas, one might, at best, learn what transformations the human organs and powers can undergo through various experiments; but they bear no direct relation to freedom from all suffering and the attainment of the soul's eternal peace. Violent sacrifice or self-mortifying tapas is not the path to nirvāṇa. The path to nirvāṇa means the destruction of craving, and the means are simply these, according to one's conviction:

A kuśalasyākaraṇe kuśalasyopasaṁpadā | Sacittapariyādapana etad Buddhānuśāsanam || (To cease from evil, to cultivate good, to purify one's mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.)

Kaunḍinya: In this hermitage, wert thou not to show me the wondrous forms of self-mortification?

Siddhartha: Come, enter within! (The curtain opens.) Siddhartha: Behold these types of self-mortification for every occasion, from the hairs of the head to the nails of the feet! See these Keśī (Hair-keepers). They consider it a sin to remove even a single hair. See their hairy bodies, as if draped in an old mat, with hair from the head reaching their backs and faces, from the nose to their moustaches, from their moustaches to their beards, and from their beards to their stomachs, and from their armpits to their ribs!

Kaunḍinya: But who is this, angrily tearing out his matted locks? Has some grievous news reached him, perhaps?

Siddhartha: Nay. He is an adherent of the Keśaluñcaka (Hair-pluckers) sect, quite opposite to the Keśī sect. They consider it a sin to leave even a single hair on the body. Moreover, since hair removed by a kṣurikā (knife) would not constitute true self-mortification, they first grow their hair long, then tear it out hair by hair with handfuls, plucking each one out.

Kaunḍinya: Who are these, raising their hands as if calling someone?

Siddhartha: That later. First, behold these, who deem it meritorious to keep their arms hanging down their whole lives, just as they were born. They never raise their arms. As a result, their bones wither, and their arms cannot move forward, backward, or upward. Opposite to them, behold these true ascetics. Their belief is that true tapas means continually holding their arms aloft against nature. By keeping both arms constantly raised, they have shrivelled like wood. How can one say which of these mutually opposing paths truly yields merit?

Kaunḍinya: But who are these, licking the ground?

Siddhartha: These are performing the Mṛgavrata (Deer-vow). They walk always on all fours, like animals. They sleep and sit like them and subsist on grass and leaves from the ground. Behold these Agatika (Motionless ones). They sit perpetually in one place. In the rain, mud accumulates around them, forming anthills, in which snakes take residence. They survive if someone puts food in their mouths; sometimes snakes show them affection, sometimes they bite and kill them. Behold these Satata Gatika (Constantly Moving ones), quite opposite to the Agatika. They are constantly in motion. If they stay in one place, they will spin around and around; but they will not cease movement. They become accustomed to sleeping while walking forward, or walking even in sleep. Ascetics observing completely opposing rules consider their respective rules with equal stubbornness to be meritorious and leading to liberation. Now, if the vow of motion is meritorious, then the vow of motionlessness must be sinful; and if motionlessness is meritorious, then constant motion is sinful! One of them is certainly mistaken, and most likely, both are mistaken; the joyful thing is only that these greatly restrained ascetics perform their chosen observances side by side, without opposing seekers of an entirely opposite conviction. Kaunḍinya, how many kinds of vows shall I tell thee? Fifty types merely concerning food. Some, to conquer the sense of taste, squeeze extremely bitter juices into every food they eat; some are Nirāśana (Fasters), eating nothing at all; while others are Sarvāśana (Omnivorous). They consider it meritorious to eat whatever appears before them when hungry, even if it be excrement, which they devour with equanimity. Some constantly sit amidst five fires, while others remain perpetually in cold water. See this one, renowned as the most prominent among these self-mortifying ascetics. He has driven sharp nails into the bottom of his sandals and plunges his feet onto their points as he walks. He purifies his eyes by igniting a fumigation of chillies and suspending himself. He burned his genitals on a heated griddle; and now, finding these pains of self-mortification insufficient, that extremely austere ascetic is eating thorns and will perpetually lie upon a bed bristling with spikes.

Kaunḍinya: Enough, Kaunḍinya! Enough! O Bodhisattva Siddhartha, I have no need whatsoever for further information about these dreadful sects!

Siddhartha: They say that if a man commits sin in this world, he must suffer such dreadful punishments in hell. But these innocent people, mistaking the infernal stone of sin for merit, voluntarily endure those torments here on earth. And they consider suffering such hellish agonies to be an easy path to heaven, to freedom, to liberation. Behold, this is mere intellectual delusion! Kaunḍinya, did thy mother love thee? Was she compassionate?

Kaunḍinya: Sire, she was most affectionate. A mother, indeed! How can I describe her love?

Siddhartha: Then would she rejoice if thou wert hungry, ate grass, or burned thy hand in the hearth; or would her wish be that thou shouldst eat thy fill, be robust and content?

Kaunḍinya: Assuredly, that I should be well-fed, joyful, and healthy –

Siddhartha: Well, Kaunḍinya, these folk consider God to be compassionate and the parent of His subjects, do they not? Is it then possible that such a compassionate parent would be pleased by starving His devotee to emaciation or burning him on a heated griddle? A god who is more pleased the more a living being is tormented must be a demon, not a god, must he not? Perform these acts for wondrous siddhis (supernatural powers); but to observe these dreadful vows and fasts, believing that a compassionate God is pleased by self-mortification or sacrificial violence and that liberation is thereby attained, is sheer folly. To me, who set forth to alleviate the world's suffering, to forcibly plunge the world into the suffering of these dreadful vows seems but cruelty.

A Disciple: (entering) — The Saṅgha (community of monks) is prepared to depart, according to the command of the Tathāgata Buddha to journey to Kapilavastu, his birthplace.

Siddhartha: Very well. Kaunḍinya, come, our aged father, King Śuddhodana, has wasted away and become utterly frail since we left the kingdom without his knowledge and went to the forest. Yielding to his summons to visit him at least once before his imminent demise, we have resolved to visit our birthplace, the capital of the Śākya nation. Moreover, there is a possibility that this personal opportunity may serve a greater global purpose. We shall strive to the utmost to crown with success our ardent desire to eliminate warfare, violence, strife, and discord from this world, and to establish everywhere a righteous kingdom of dharma (righteous duty), by imparting the teaching of the Four Noble Truths we discovered to the Śākya nation, just as the Kings of Kosala and Magadha became followers of the Tathāgata Buddha, and by making the royal family and military commanders of the Śākya nation our adherents. Kaunḍinya, if all mankind comprehends that there is no suffering like worldly existence, then why would wars and conflicts arise for the illusory gains of this exceedingly painful world? Just as no wise man contends to be bitten by a venomous serpent, so no living creature will contend to leap into the pyre of this worldly existence. Kaunḍinya, truly, there is no suffering like worldly craving. There is no happiness like dispassionate renunciation. Behold—look at that distant mountain, see how the forest fire blazes!

Song:

Song Details: Title: To vaṇavā bagh dūrī Chāl: Tū Ānabān Velī Original: तो वणवा बघ दूरी । जीव जंतु जाळी । भडकत दशदिशा । आग ।। ध्रु. ।। पेटत पळ पळ तैसा । तृष्णाग्नीत । संसार जळत हाय ॥ १ ॥ Translation: Behold that distant forest fire / It burns all creatures, / The flames rage in all directions. (Chorus) Like that, moment by moment, / This worldly existence burns / In the fire of craving, alas!

[End of Scene 1]

docs.title: Scene 2
docs.text:
Kshara is seated. Just then, Shankambhat enters.

Shankambhat: Kshara, again you have come onto the osari (verandah) and seated yourself with such abandon! All and sundry will come onto the osari; the osari is a public market place, and there you sit. Now, if I were to combine these two words and call you by that name, you would claim I abuse you! The proper place for women to sit is the saipakghar (kitchen).

Kshara: Silence, you chagalkutle (babbler)! If I am not to sit upon the osari, then what shall I do? You say women's place is in the saipakghar, but what accursed difference is there between a saipakghar and an osari when not a single grain of food have you ever procured to cook in that very saipakghar! If you, like other industrious men, were to make the rupees clink and jingle upon the osari, then I too would be busied with domestic chores in the saipakghar like other settled women. But what accursed stone has God bound about my neck! My life has been squandered. Else, I would have graced the throne as queen to some king.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Joda Mam Kiti Vijod Chāl: Ari Rang Range Gyan Original: जोडा मम किती विजोड । हे ठब्बु मी छान । मी गाय । हे गिधाड । हे बदसुर । मी तान ।। ध्रु. ।। गूळचि मी चव ज्याला । त्याचि न हे तेचि जाण । मज पूर्ण मज समचि । पति दे न भगवान् ।। १ ।। Translation: How mismatched is my pair! He, a dullard; I, comely. I, a song; he, a vulture. He, off-key; I, the melody. (Chorus) I am the jaggery that has taste, But its flavour, he perceives not. To me, one wholly like myself, A husband, God does not grant.

Shankambhat: What is it you say, Kshara! Are you in your senses! Do you truly believe you ought to have obtained a husband exactly like you (‘tujasamachi pati’), a perfectly suitable husband? Foolish woman! If that were so, you would weep. If your husband were exactly like you, then though called a man, he would be but a woman! Those who bless maidens with 'may you obtain a suitable groom (‘anurupa varapraptiraastu’)' know not the calamity (anartha) implicit in their words. Nay, there is a slight, inherent mismatch by birth between women and men, and therefore their marital bond is formed. For this reason, give thanks to God that your husband is thus somewhat mismatched with you, not entirely suited to you. Were it otherwise, Kshara, you would be weeping, verily weeping.

Kshara: And now what else have I but my divinely ordained weeping! Great was your father’s laukik (reputation) as a priest. But you have brought it to dust with your extravagance and idleness. The custom (vritti) of rich citizens has vanished, yet these few rustic folk still come to our door; I thought we might earn a few coins by telling them some sankalp bikalp (ritual intentions and such)! Shall I bid them enter then? They have made two rounds already. In such a state, with naught to eat nor to scratch for in the house, it is not seemly to only perform the duties of a priest when a wealthy patron (yajaman) is present.

Shankambhat: What you say is quite right. This is not a question of wealth. This is primarily a question of shraddha (faith). Shraddha does not depend on wealth, but on how much of his wealth one is prepared to donate, to offer as dakshina (honorarium). Many rich folk begrudge even offering a betel nut; whereas many an impoverished soul, even at the cost of his very life, will not fail to give dakshina with cupped hands full. Thus, the measure of a man's religious shraddha is not how much dakshina he can give, but how much dakshina he desires to give—how much he desires to give in cash. Go, measure their shraddha by that scale! Bring in the faithful one who has brought the most dakshina. Drive away the other faithless ones. Kshara, go, tell them this is the command of your husband, Shankambhat.

Kshara: But how can one succeed by focusing solely on dakshina! What if someone has no dakshina—

Shankambhat: Then it should be understood that he lacks shraddha.

Kshara: But are not these ten patrons coming to our door because we are mendicant priests (bhikshuk)? Yet—

Shankambhat: Enough of your 'buts' and 'however's! You say ten patrons come to the door! Women should call but one man their master. I alone am patron enough. Go. Wait! Look, the one who gives the most dakshina must also be ashikshit (unlettered). Just as you dislike a pearl heavier than your nose, so I do not favour a patron more learned than the priest. Go!

Ksharabai exits and brings in an ignorant farmer.

Farmer: I bow at your feet, O divine one.

Shankambhat: Blessings (Kalyan). (To Kshara) You, go inside now. I said go, did I not! I do not approve of women standing thus upon the osari before another man.

Kshara: Here, I go, once and for all!

Shankambhat: (Aside) He appears to be a rustic indeed. (Aloud) Is it a teerthvidhi (pilgrimage ritual) you wish to perform, or a shraddha (ancestral ritual), or a snansankalp (ritualistic bath vow)! Why do you stumble so? These Sanskrit names for rituals, you, a rustic, may not comprehend, so I shall ask you in the common tongue (prakrit). Listen! How many rupees have you brought as dakshina? Forty, or thirty, or twenty?

Farmer: (Aside) Ah, so? I must teach him a little common parlance by seizing this chance. (Aloud) O divine one, I have brought five rupees as dakshina.

Shankambhat: Then in all of Sanskrit literature, there is no religious rite (dharmavidhi) by that name. Ten rupees are the minimum required!

Farmer: Very well, O divine one, I shall manage to give that much somehow.

Shankambhat: Good. That ritual which in prakrit is called 'ten rupees', in Sanskrit it is called a snansankalp. Come, be prepared for the pilgrimage vow (teerthsankalp)!

Farmer: But one must go to a pilgrimage site (teerth), no?

Shankambhat: Foolish fellow. Every priest's house is itself a teerth! If I sprinkle water with sacred grass (darbha), you gain the merit (punya) of an ordinary teerth. If I sprinkle it with my finger, you gain the punya of bathing directly in the Bhagirathi. Come, you recite the vow (sankalp). I shall sprinkle the water. Then you may go to the river and take dips all day, or never bathe again in your entire life. You will assuredly gain the punya of bathing. Come. Sit cross-legged. Take out your dakshina, count it, place it here; join your hands. Whatever word I tell you, pronounce it clearly. When I make hand gestures, you must make them too, mind you! Speak, what is your name? Hmm. Om Namah—

Farmer: Speak, what is your name? Hmm. Om Namah!

Shankambhat: No, no. Say what your name is, then say Om Namah!

Farmer: No, no. Say what your name is, then say Om Namah!

Shankambhat: Your name first; then Om Namah.

Farmer: Your name first; then Om Namah.

Shankambhat: Curse you! Just Om Namah!

Farmer: Curse you! Just Om Namah!

Shankambhat: What a donkey you are!

Farmer: What a donkey you are!

Shankambhat: You paji (rascal)!

Farmer: You paji!

Shankambhat: Your father is a paji.

Farmer: Your father is a paji.

Shankambhat: (Picking up the dakshina) Thief!

Farmer: (Snatching the dakshina) Thief!

Shankambhat: Take that! (He delivers a punch)

Farmer: Take that! (Delivers a return punch)

Finally, they come to blows. The Farmer seizes Shankambhat by the ear, forcing his neck down and bending him.

Shankambhat: Ayayayi! Oh, run to my aid! Oh Mother, oh Mother!

Kshara peeks through the doorway and runs away. Shankambhat: Oh, come back, why do you go! Oh Mother!

Kshara: You are calling out to your Mother, are you not? Then your Mother shall descend from heaven; you said again, you do not like women to come onto the osari.

Shankambhat: Oh, I do like it—Good heavens! Oh! Not Mother, you come! You, Kshara, O Madam Ksharabai, O Madam Ksharabai Maharaj! Come quickly!

Kshara: (Entering) O Farmer-gentleman, release him! Forgive whatever he may have said, for my sake. His tongue is a trifle fatkal (sharp-tongued). Have mercy!

The Farmer releases his ear. Shankambhat rushes headlong into the house. The Farmer bows to Ksharabai and departs.

Shankambhat: (Taking an old sword, peeking cautiously from behind the doorway) Oh, is he gone?

Kshara smiles and nods, indicating 'he's gone', whereupon Shankambhat emerges and speaks loudly. Shankambhat: Is he gone indeed! Where did the coward (bhyad) flee? What shall I do! Had he been here now, I would have torn him to pieces, verily pieces! Why did you release him? I had given my ear into his hand to test you! You believed it true and said before my enemy that I was fatkal of tongue! And now you have bid my enemy flee, granting him life (pranadan). I understand your deceit (kapat). Kshara, did you speak with another man (parpurusha)? A husband is the king of his wife! You have betrayed him (droh)! Therefore, according to the strictures of treason (rajvidroha chya nirbandhanusar), I shall sever your head! You said my tongue is fatkal, no; my sword is more fatkal than my tongue. Speak, why did you intervene? What if that coward were to come here now! Coward, come forth, let me see!—

Farmer: (Re-entering, rebuking) What?

Shankambhat: (Hiding the sword behind his back and discarding it, he retreats behind Kshara and nudges her) I thought he had gone far away! Oh, intervene, intervene, appease him!

Kshara: I shall not appease him! Women should not even stand and speak with another man; to intervene in their affairs is out of the question.

Shankambhat: When commanded by one's husband, there is no harm in standing and speaking with another man, nay, even in intervening. Appease him! Seeing his eyes, whirling like a chakra, Kshara, my head spins and I feel dizzy.

Kshara: Good man, you may go now! Seeing his pitiful state, you should feel amusement rather than anger. Go now, good sir!

The Farmer bows and departs; just then, Baan enters.

Shankambhat: Who? Baan! Was it not your guard upon the ramparts of Prince Siddhartha’s pleasure-palace, he who is now called Buddha? What an unfortunate man, that Siddhartha, this Buddha of today. He preferred to roll in the ashes of a cremation ground rather than upon a bed of flowers with beauties, each more exquisite than Yashodhara!

Baan: He found it agreeable; but his abandoned wife, Devi Yashodhara, is weeping bitterly. Her plight is truly pitiful.

Shankambhat: Oh, hear you not, how wretched is the plight of women when abandoned by their husbands! Therefore, I tell you, cherish me, else—

Kshara: What, else what? Because her husband was a great, valiant prince, Yashodhara was heartbroken when he abandoned her for the forest. But women upon whose neck such a burden (khes) falls, they, on the contrary, feel like making vows, making vows, that their husbands should at least have the sense to go into exile! Yes, if a husband whose companionship is truly joyous accepts exile, then it is sorrow! But as for husbands by whose fault the domestic life of women like me becomes as arduous as exile—why do they not go into exile today, if they are to go tomorrow? Will you go now?

Shankambhat: I would have gone; but as you say, since our domestic life is itself exile, what distinction remains in exile now! There are wild boars in the forest, and (pointing at Kshara) are there none here, pray?

Kshara: (Pointing at Shankambhat) —Indeed there are! Who but a wild boar would perform such an act as you have just done, burying your snout in the mud of slander against a hero of renunciation (tyagaveer) like Siddhartha, this Buddha?

Shankambhat: Tyagaveer! Oh, pray tell! What unprecedented renunciation (apurva tyag) did Siddhartha perform that you now call him a tyagaveer! After indulging in all pleasures from birth until satiation, anyone would grow disgusted. After experiencing the passionate delights of youth, day and night for thirty years, in the cool embraces of numerous moon-faced beauties (chandranana), each more exquisite than Yashodhara, that he should then feel a slight chill and wish to warm himself by a forest fire for a while—what wonder is there in that, and what heroism (veeratva)? Let alone thirty years; but if anyone were to appoint me commander-in-chief of the host of beauties in such a pleasure-palace for at least thirty days, on condition of then departing for exile, I would sign that agreement right now! Let me revel in such a pleasure-palace for thirty days, and as its month's rent, I shall happily walk into the forest on the thirty-first day. But how shall our desire for a home be fulfilled? The lot that has fallen to us is such a character! What wonder then that our unsatiated ghosts of sensual pleasures should still hover around the domestic sphere? And oh, oh, just because Siddhartha, this Buddha, abandoned Yashodhara and left, it is not as if he has abandoned the world entirely! His Highness has merely gone off somewhere for a couple of days to taste piquant, astringent, and sour chutneys, having grown weary of the rich delicacies of royal pleasures. He will certainly return! If he returns as a king, then the royal harem (ranivasa) is here; if he returns as an ascetic (bairagi), then they will make her adopt the garb of an ascetic (bairagini) herself. It is all one and the same. Oh, oh, men cannot but keep women (kamini), these jewels among women (striratne), on their persons, under one pretext or another. Be he a householder, or one living in seclusion in a forest retreat, without women (kaminiwachun), they may last perhaps four days; but on the fifth day, back they come for penance (prayashchitta)! Be they one who chants prayers (japi), one who performs penance (tapi), one with a topknot (shikhi), or a renunciate (sannyasi); some will keep a beloved wife, others a beloved disciple (priya shishya)! Some as a lover (anuragini), others as a female ascetic (bairagini)! Ramachandra was a slave to Janaki's lotus-face, and Hanuman to her lotus-feet—but all told, slaves to women (lalnanche das)! Therefore, do not be in such haste to create such a fuss (stom majavun) about Siddhartha Gautama’s exile and deride us householders. If this Buddha does not return for Yashodhara, today or tomorrow, then my name is not Shankambhat!

Kshara: Silence! You have a habit of slandering any great man you see.

Shankambhat: Silence! You have a habit of calling anyone I slander great.

Kshara: Today, even in the heat of slandering Siddhartha, you have at least acknowledged that men are slaves to women, have you not?

Shankambhat: Yes, to women; but not to such a slave-woman as that!

Baan: Reverend Priest! I have some urgent business (nikadiche kaam). You know that I am a sentinel on the ramparts around the pleasure-palace. The day Siddhartha fled, I am accused of leaving the palace gates open. For years, I have bought time by one means or another, but now time will surely claim me. They say the King will inflict capital punishment (prandand) upon me. No counsel comes to mind.

Kshara: So you came to him to seek counsel, did you?

Baan: No, Madam, do not be angry! How can I seek the wrong thing in the wrong place; but I heard the reputation that the Reverend Priest gives tait (amulet) consecrated with mantras to ward off calamities, so I came.

Shankambhat: An tait for the calamity of capital punishment, eh? At least five tola (tola - a unit of weight) of gold are required?

Baan: B-b-b-b! Will three tolas not suffice?

Shankambhat: My good man, is the body you wish to save made of three great elements? The body is made of five great elements (panchamahabhuta), so five tolas of gold! Come, produce the money—

Baan: I refer you to Seth Sunas.

Shankambhat: Seth Sunas? We are their hereditary priests (pidhijata upadhyaya). Excellent. Well, now you must say that a rumour (gapp) has spread in the village that some wondrous (adbhut) things happened on the night Siddhartha fled; do you know of any such adbhut occurrence?

Baan: Yes, indeed, one adbhut thing did truly happen. That night, before the rampart gates were closed, while I stood guard, I felt like sitting, then like sleeping, and then fell into a deep slumber! But how can I recount this adbhut thing?

Shankambhat: (Laughing) Bravo, Baana, bravo! In short, you dozed off and slept on duty—is that not the adbhut thing? Well, did anything else adbhut occur?

Baan: Nothing else happened!

Shankambhat: It did.

Baan: It did not, Maharaj!

Shankambhat: Baana, do you wish to live or to die?

Baan: To live, Maharaj.

Shankambhat: Then say it happened. An adbhut thing hap-pened.

Baan: It happened. An adbhut thing happened. But which one?

Shankambhat: It is this: that while you were on guard, you closed the gates. You secured the bolts, locks, latches, and hooks with a clatter. But just then, an angel came and passed his hand over your eyes and said, "Be unconscious!" And you all fell unconscious, and upon waking at dawn, found the doors still firmly shut. You remember nothing of what transpired in between; you must say this by rote! My tait will do the rest.

Baan: But—

Shankambhat: Silence. This is precisely what you must say. Oh, you fool, to ward off the public scandal (lokapavad) of these naive, faithful folk, the shield of divine miracle proves useful. The maiden Kunti (upavar Kunti) bore a child before marriage. Public scandal arose! In reality, there was no exception in it. It is merely a natural law. But when it was seen that lokapavad concerning the illegitimate son (kanin putra) was inevitable, Vyasa cleverly threw in the tale of the divine miracle of the Sun-mantra, and the foolish doubts were satisfied by a cunning answer. So too shall it be today. Not only this, but if in time Siddhartha Gautama truly becomes a great founder of a religion, then even in the new Puranas of his followers, this fanciful tale (bhakad katha) I have suggested will attain great glory as a religious story (dharmakatha). Though my name may not shine in that Purana like Vyasa's, who is to say it will not float upon the narrative stream and land upon the shores of future generations! Well, come inside, I will give you the tait.

They exit.

docs.title: Scene 3
docs.text:
(King Shuddhodan stands.)

Senapati Vikramsingh: All hail King Shuddhodan!

Shuddhodan: Welcome! Senapati Vikramsingh, welcome! Is the news brought by yesterday's merchants indeed true? Has it been confirmed that my son Siddhartha, who left me long ago, is returning to meet me, having attained the honour of a Jagadguru (world teacher)?

Vikramsingh: Most certainly! After your son Siddhartha, wearied, renounced the kingdom with the noble aim of liberating the world from all suffering, he undertook an exceedingly severe penance of self-mortification. However, upon realising that the austerities of self-mortification were not the primary means to moksha (liberation), he set forth to attain his goal through the path of knowledge, and eventually achieved the supreme siddhi (accomplishment) of samādhi (meditative absorption). Nevertheless, even whilst enjoying the self-contentment of having attained nirvana (cessation of suffering), he began to wander, instructing the world in the path to nirvana solely for the welfare of mankind. It is his unshakeable conviction that he has discovered the path to free humanity from the clutches of birth, death, old age, and sickness. Thousands of people, kings, and great kings are becoming devotees of Buddha. However, since the principal guiding tenet of Bhagavan Buddha's supremely generous and profoundly compassionate dharma (righteous duty) is ‘pariṇāma-tāpa-saṁskārād guṇavṛtti-virodhāchcha sarvameva duḥkhe vivekinaḥ’, his doctrine holds that this sorrowful world should be renounced as swiftly as possible, and that complete renunciation is only achievable through sanyasa (renunciation). In like manner, their act of imparting sanyasa to thousands of people is, I believe, detrimental to the welfare of mankind, and it was for this very reason that I intended to discuss it with him upon his arrival. Fortunately, the opportune moment for that direct meeting has arrived today. Bhagavan Buddha, having set forth to revisit his capital, Kapilavastu, is now close to the city.

Shuddhodan: Ah, today my son Siddhartha shall meet me after a separation of nine or ten years! In my old age, he is my sole staff and support. Upon his arrival, I shall bestow upon him the royal consecration of this crown, and I shall embrace the sanyasa-diksha (initiation into renunciation) myself. Is the capital splendidly adorned? Upon his arrival, there shall be dances, cymbals, trumpets, horns, drums— Hark! A chaughada (a set of four musical instruments used in processions) sounds, but why has it ceased? How will my son appear? How will he conduct himself? Every moment seems an aeon to me!

(A messenger enters.)

Vikramsingh: Why has the chaughada sounded but once, then ceased? Has Siddhartha been sighted from the city's perimeter?

Messenger: Sighted, you ask? Your Majesty, he has already entered the city!

Shuddhodan: Then why have not the ten directions yet resounded with welcoming instruments and acclamations for my son? What a grave error!

Messenger: Forgive me, Your Majesty! But the chaughada at the perimeter gate, which was to give the first signal, was silenced by Siddhartha himself as soon as the first beat fell, thus confusing the people at the city gates. Each time the chaughadas attempted to resume, Siddhartha had them silenced again. Meanwhile, leaving the main gateway, Prince Siddhartha entered the city by a side path; avoiding the designated and adorned route for his procession, he deliberately proceeded through the squalid, narrow, and outcast lanes where the humble, poor, and untouchables reside, soliciting and accepting alms. And an immense multitude stands frozen along the main thoroughfare, gazing at the sight with astonishment!

Shuddhodan: What? My son, the heir of King Shuddhodan, the Crown Prince of this Shakya nation, wandering through his own capital, begging for alms at the doors of untouchables? Has this thorn brought disgrace upon my entire lineage? Born into a Kshatriya (warrior class) royal clan, yet begs for alms! He takes food from those whose very shadow is considered Vitāḷ (defilement/pollution)! Oh, messenger, how dared those untouchables offer him alms? How felt they no fear of my wrath?

Messenger: Your Majesty, to Buddhadeva—

Shuddhodan: Who is this Buddha? What Buddha? What sort of Buddha? He is Siddhartha Gautama. Therefore, at least in my presence, he must be called Siddhartha.

Messenger: My apologies! None but Your Majesty alone possesses the power to deter Siddhartha from this contact with the food of untouchables.

Shuddhodan: Chief Minister, bring my horse at once! This impropriety must be halted by me! Though I have grown old, I am still the King of the Shakyas. This rebellious conduct of Siddhartha, which stains the honour and creed of that proud nation and lineage, must be punished by me! Bring the horse, go! Go! And command the people to clear the path. Else, I shall not hesitate to charge my horse headlong through the throng.

docs.title: Scene 4
docs.text:
(Shākambhatji’s House; Shākambhat is seated, Kṣhārā enters crying loudly.)

Kṣhārā: Heard you, pray? There is no rice, no rice! Ten days have passed; there are not four grains even in the house. That which I brought from my father’s house, you have devoured greedily until now, but they have now steadfastly declared that they will not provide even a morsel (śīta) from tomorrow. Therefore, I say, my lord, ‘No rice, no rice!’ Have you heard me now, at last?

Shākambhat: Good heavens! Then, my dearest, why did you not apprise me yesterday, just as you have now gently informed me? Kṣhārā, this is no jest; in this one day, I shall surely procure a thousand rupees. I, your husband, I shall procure it. Regarding Prince Siddhārtha’s escape, I had given a charm (tāīta) to Bāṇa, for which Sunās Śeṭjī had stood guarantee, but that wretched fellow had not yet paid me a single pai (coin). I have him in a bind now. I shall demand a thousand, a full thousand!

Kṣhārā: You may demand ten thousand, but will he agree to pay when the time comes! Though that Śeṭjī be simple-minded, he is a miser. Furthermore, you owe him a thousand already. He is certain to deduct it from that sum.

Shākambhat: Oh, those bonds I shall surely tear up; but on top of that, I shall take another thousand in cash! Even that merchant (vāṇī), along with the villagers, calls me a mischievous fellow (kuṭāḷ). Very well, if mischievous, then mischievous! I shall make that Śeṭjī beat the cymbals, only then shall I truly earn the name of kuṭāḷ! What is his name again, Sunās Śeṭ—

Kṣhārā: Why? The name Sunās truly suits that Śeṭjī, does it not? His nose is indeed quite sharp, is it not?

Shākambhat: Hmph, oh, I say, this habit of yours to examine whether other men’s noses are sharp or flabby, their eyes bright or rheumy, I shall not tolerate it in the least. You are well past your twenty-fifth year. It is high time to abandon this frivolous (caṭorpaṇā) habit of scrutinising every passing man’s countenance.

Kṣhārā: If such be your wrath, then be calm, my lord. For that Śeṭjī’s sharp nose I had observed furtively when I was but twenty years of age, not twenty-five, you see. Then there is no harm, is there? And as for frivolousness, what frivolousness is there in us women looking at men who come and go? Do not we women look at the crows, dogs, and buffaloes in the street—so too do we look at you men. When fifty-six men from various lands gather around a single maiden to perform the respectable thuggery of a svayaṁvara (a ceremony where a maiden chooses her husband), what brawls, what blows, what wrestling—even cats and dogs, accursed creatures, fight their shameless quarrels with more decorum than your Sītā svayaṁvara, and Rukmiṇī svayaṁvara, or our Siddhārtha Buddha’s Yaśodharā svayaṁvara! Have five or fifty women ever gathered and displayed such base fawning before one man? If a man’s nose, prominent like a village fort, is casually seen by a woman’s eyes, it becomes her shamelessness. But your men? The hundred Kauravas even disrobed their own sister-in-law in a full assembly to render her naked—was that the civility of men!-

Song:

Song Details: Title: While a shameless woman speaks Chāl: Adakh Bhujtayā Kheliye Original: निलाजरी स्त्री वदताना । लाज कशी वाटे न नरांना ।। ध्रु. ।। नग्न करू नरा कधि का लाखो । स्त्रिया झोंबल्या हासत खो खो । द्रौपदीस नर जैसे नाना ॥ १ Translation: While a shameless woman speaks aloud, Why do not men feel any shame? (Chorus) Have millions of women ever Clung laughing to men to make them bare? As did men of Draupadī, with cruel aim.

Kṣhārā: The spittle that dripped from the mouths of great sages upon merely beholding us women has soaked every single page of your Purāṇas, soaked it through! No sooner did the writers of the Purāṇas espy a woman, than they began to gush in her description—beautiful, with lovely hair (sukeśī), fair-faced (sumukhī), with fine teeth (sudatī), slender-waisted (sumadhyamā), broad-hipped (pṛuthujaṅghanā), lion-waisted (siṁhakaṭī)—as if these wretches had measured every limb and feature of all those women! Siṁhakaṭī and pṛuthujaṅghanā are far-fetched indeed; but should anyone merely call me Rambhorū (having thighs like a plantain tree), I would even take off my sandal and strike them with it!

Shākambhat: You speak well. If any man who beholds you were to call you Rambhorū, Siṁhakaṭī, or some such thing, then I too (pointing at her) shall take out my own sandal! And I shall expose his blindness! Yes, let someone call you Siṁhamukhī (lion-faced) if they will—but what is Siṁhakaṭī? Sudatī, Subhrū (with beautiful eyebrows), Sundarī (beautiful woman), Sukeśā—anyone who dares to affix the prefix ‘su’ to any limb, body part, minor limb, or feature, or combination thereof, of yours, I shall compel him to sigh in regret many a time! As for the rest, if ever the occasion arises to compose a Purāṇa about you, then, by your good fortune, a new sage has indeed emerged who describes things exactly to your liking. You women need no longer fear the perspective of the old Vyāsa who called women sumukhī. This new sage is Prince Siddhārtha Gautama! He has attained Buddhahood, they say? He would not even grant you or any woman the honour of being mentioned as sumukhī, let alone durmukhī (ill-faced). For he does not wish to behold your countenances at all. He reportedly states that to gaze upon a woman’s face is a sin! The Buddha intensely despises this inauspicious female body, with your runny, mucous-filled noses and foul-smelling mouths—he does not even permit you women, born of sin (pāpayoni), to stand in the wind!

Kṣhārā: If any creature were to call women pāpayoni a couple of years before its own birth, then I might perchance call it a virtuous man (puṇyapurūṣa). But he who, having once been born from a woman’s womb, then calls women unclean, with that very sentence bestows upon himself the esteemed title of a worm in the filth. The guru-mahārājās who declare that the female body is inauspicious and that women should not be permitted to stand in the wind—the breeze around their throngs of disciples is surely as fragrant and auspicious as the Malaya breeze, is it not? And the guru’s own body? Then why should others stand in the breeze of these gurus’ bodies! Yet people are meant to drink the holy water (tīrtha) from their feet! When phlegm flows from women’s noses, and when your Vyāsas, Vālmīkis, or some Buddhas catch a cold—and even Gautama Buddha, who set out to dispel the world’s afflictions, reportedly catches colds—does then sacred water flow from their noses like the Gaṅgotrī and Bhāgīrathī? Then why do you not perform ācaman (ritual sipping of water) with their effluvium at your evening prayers? And perhaps you do, madam. For was it not just the other day that some paramahaṁsa (a renunciate of the highest order) arrived, who condemned women as unclean? He reportedly always lay stretched on his bed. Therein he performed his bodily functions, and at the appointed time, he himself ate his own excrement and urine and smeared it on the mouths of his disciples! But that was the guru-mahārājā’s filth; it was prasāda (a blessed offering)! It must have tasted very sweet, no? You too had gone there; did you not partake of a little? Those pigs, accursed creatures, are better than such men. Fie upon it! Oh, but I was forgetting. You told me what the Buddha says about women, but you did not tell me what women, in turn, offer the Buddha by way of retort, did you? Just yesterday, a woman from Magadha came. When the Buddha came to her village, he took the devout children of those who offered him alms into his mendicant order, and those homes were ruined. His disciples boasted that their guru cured the whole world of disease and suffering. And lo and behold, in that very village, the Buddha guru fell so ill with a cold that words cannot describe it? Then even the village women and folk began to make up amusing songs about him and sing them. That woman even sang a song for me—oh, madam, it was just like this:

Song:

Song Details: Title: My guru, madam Chāl: Calo Re Māyī Auvāliyā Original: माझा ग गुरू बाई । भीक दे जो । भिकारी त्यासचि करि पाही ।। ध्रु. ।। अवघ्या जगवू जगासि आला । पडशापायी आपण मेला । वरही जयाचा बरवा । शाप म्हणवी ।। १ Translation: My guru, madam, he who asks For alms, makes a beggar of him he finds. (Chorus) Come to save the entire world, He himself was undone by a cold. His blessing, though fair, a curse it finds.

Shākambhat: It was not for nothing that I called you Siṁhamukhī! Very well, oh, I say, now be a little ‘gomukhī’ (cow-faced, implying docile/quiet); see, Sunās Śeṭ is coming this way. His mother is at death’s door, and seizing this opportunity, I have concocted a grand scheme. I shall count out the money from him, clink-clink. Go inside, go. (Kṣhārā exits.)

Sunāsśeṭ: (Entering) Shākambhat, my good fellow, now at least employ some divine remedy, some charm or other! My mother, alas, will not survive this day. She is about to leave me! Not that her condition is dire. She had been languishing in old age, a mere lump; it is a release for her. But I shall lose my mother! (He sobs.)

Shākambhat: (Suddenly wailing) And she will leave me too! She was my mother as well. Śeṭjī, no, no, Dādā (elder brother), brother, I swear to you that you are my own stepbrother, and your mother is my stepmother! Why do you stare with your mouth agape thus? Dādā, when a secret of your—of our—lineage, hitherto concealed, is unveiled today, you will not be surprised that I hold you in the same regard as I do myself! Oh, brother, my father and yours were one and the same. Your real father is my stepfather, and she, my mother, is now leaving me. (He weeps.)

Sunāsśeṭ: What is it you say? What step-relation? What brother? Have you gone mad? Shākambhat, I forgive you because you are our family’s hereditary priest (upādhyāya). Otherwise, I would not tolerate such nonsensical babble and utterly impudent words merely because of our familiarity.

Shākambhat: I too would not have spoken—but Dādā, it is not merely familiarity; our homes are one. See here what it is. My father gave me this charm (tāīta) upon his deathbed and instructed me that when Sunās Śeṭjī’s mother begins to die, on that very day, I should open this tāīta. Both of us were to read the letter within and both were to offer her water. We were to burn this letter on her funeral pyre. Otherwise, my spirit would become a ghost and hover around both your houses! Therefore, today I broke open the tāīta, opened the letter, and understood the secret! Brother. When your first father passed away, was your mother in Kāśī? Was she delivered of you after his passing?

Sunāsśeṭ: (Angrily) She was, well then? Speak, tell me what it is, at once.

Shākambhat: Then all this is true. My father was there, with her, as her upādhyāya. There, your mother bore a son by him. That is you. You are my brother, just as the charitable Karṇa was to the virtuous Yudhiṣṭhira! Therefore, I say, not my father’s, nay, our father’s—

Sunāsśeṭ: I shall knock out your teeth!

Shākambhat: Knock out my teeth. But as long as I have a tongue, brother, I shall read this letter aloud to all during the old woman’s funeral procession, and I shall offer her water! My father had two wishes: that I should repay the five or six thousand rupees owed to him by your household, so that he might be freed from debt (ṛṇa) and attain salvation (gati). And this was the second wish. Of these two, I must fulfill at least one. Otherwise, his spirit will remain entangled and wander about both you and me as a ghost! If the debt is settled, it is well; otherwise, even if it costs me my life, I shall not refrain from divulging this secret. Brother, my own, my stepbrother he is!

Sunāsśeṭ: (Pushing him away) Away! (Aside) Is this fellow’s intrigue, or his father’s, or my mother’s, truly possible? My mother was indeed at his father’s house over there. Tales of ghosts are also heard, after all. It could be true. My head is throbbing! But whatever it may be, if even a mere rumour of this reaches anyone’s ears tomorrow, people will believe it to be true; it will be difficult to cremate my mother; the whole community will rise up in protest! (Aloud) Shākambhat, you son of a donkey—

Shākambhat: Nay, brother, do not speak such foul words about your own father, for brother, whose son I am, of him are you also a son!

Sunāsśeṭ: Oh, speak softly, at least! Oh, how great is my mother’s reputation among the people! Women consider her a goddess. Do not speak such scandalous things at the time of her passing. Look, I shall relinquish what was owed to me by your father. I shall write you this receipt. Thus he will be freed from debt, and his soul will attain liberation (mukti). When this one wish is fulfilled, will that not suffice? But I swear you by God. Speak not a single word more concerning my mother after this.

Shākambhat: Oh, say ‘my mother,’ brother. Why should I defame her? Your lineage is my lineage. You yourself have become my lineage now! Then again, that same—

Sunāsśeṭ: I told you to abandon that indecency!

Shākambhat: Very well, I shall not speak. One of father’s wishes is fulfilled. That is done. Otherwise, the fear of ghosts! Give me that receipt for the debt repayment.

Sunāsśeṭ: You too write that you will not utter another word.

Shākambhat: Of course, but you too must provide a copy of it. Come inside.

Sunāsśeṭ: That is the custom of business, after all. Come! (Aside) What am I doing? But there is no recourse! Be that as it may, once my mother’s funeral rites (pretavidhi) and post-mortem rituals (aurdhvadehika) are concluded, I shall see to this village scoundrel (gāvkuṭāḷ) somewhere.

docs.title: Scene 5
docs.text:
Buddha walks, begging for alms. Citizens stand by. Just then, King Shuddhodana arrives.

Shuddhodana: Where is that Siddhartha? Where is that mendicant who defiles the royal lineage?

Siddhartha: Here he is, Your Majesty! This Siddhartha, who once caused you sorrow and who now causes blemish to your lineage, stands here, offering obeisance to his father.

Shuddhodana: My child, Siddhartha, my son, seeing you returned safely to our capital, the ocean of joy surging in my heart has drowned and dissolved all anger at this eccentricity of your mendicant ways! Oh, how humble is my son! Though he has ascended to the rank of Mahanta (Great One) and become the guru of kings and emperors, he has not forgotten his filial dharma (righteous duty). That messenger surely spoke idly, and thus I was angered for naught. You merely entered the capital through a by-path, begging for alms, as is customary for a bhikshu (Buddhist monk), is it not?

Messenger: (Aside) What more did I say, pray tell! But the fault lies not with the angered father; nor with the humble son; the fault, if any, lies with the messenger! A messenger is like a mridanga (percussion instrument), struck on both sides.

Shuddhodana: My beloved son, you have met me – in this, I have forgotten all past sorrow and grief. But my child, Siddhartha, since you left me and the kingdom to undertake penance, for nine or ten years now, I have borne the burden of this kingdom in hope of this day, which has dawned today. This burden of state, from your aged father, O humble son, do you now take upon your capable head and thus render me carefree. This jewelled crown of the Shakya kingdom, O Crown Prince, I place upon your head this day. This crown befits you, a young prince, and tonsure (shaving of the head) befits me, an old man; therefore, free our royal lineage today from the blemish of this uncanonical reversal, occasioned by your tonsure in the prime of youth and my wearing of the crown in my ripe old age. Take this crown and give that kamandalu (water-pot) hither.

Siddhartha: Halt, Your Majesty! Had I not borne another burden upon my head, then perhaps I might have borne the burden of this crown. But I believe I would not have borne it even then. For since childhood, whenever I saw impoverished and toiling farmers drenched in sweat, and soldiers wounded in battle for a king's avarice, bathed in blood, then did this royal crown fill me with disgust. I felt that every idle emerald within this crown was a drop of the sweat of those farmers and labourers, and every greedy ruby and jewel within this crown was a drop of the soldiers' blood. A king's thirst is like a rakshasi (demoness), drinking the blood of these toiling labourers. And this crown is the cup from which that demonic royal thirst drinks blood. O Crown! A kamandalu filled with drops of pure water, equal to the number of jewels within you, and a cupped palm full of grains of rice, are more useful than you. For these may be drunk by the lowly and thirsty, and eaten by the hungry. But you, most useless, shining pebbles, which cannot be drunk, nor eaten – begone! Return to the rubbish heap from which foolish men gathered you, deeming you jewels! (He attempts to cast away the crown, but the royal attendants catch it mid-air.)

Song:
