Song Details: Title: Tujahuni Mukuta Kamandalu Bara Rāga: X | Tāla: Y | Chāl: Sakal Gada Chanda Kalasan Original: तुजहुनि मुकुटा कमंडलु बरा । तू अमोल । कवडि मोल जरि हा ॥ ध्रु.।। छत्रे तव तापा । अधिक देऊन । सुकविले जीव तू । सुखवि सुजले हा ।। १ ।। Translation: O crown, the kamandalu is better than you; you are priceless, yet this is but worth a cowrie shell. (Chorus) Your canopy, giving more heat, has withered lives; this one refreshes and soothes.

Siddhartha: Your Majesty, without removing the burden of this crown from my head, where will space be found upon it to bear the burden of the world's welfare?

Shuddhodana: But Siddhartha! Verily, the Kshatriya (warrior/ruling class) lineage into which you were born has the duty of bearing the crown. At the very least, do not practice such a mendicant's life. That is not the dharma of our lineage.

Siddhartha: Your Majesty, that may not be the dharma of your lineage, but it is the dharma of mine.

Shuddhodana: O Siddhartha, in this Shakya lineage of yours, twenty-two ancestors renowned as Mahasamantas (Great Chieftains), twenty-two generations of crowned kings have passed, and not one of them was a beggar. How then do you say that mendicancy is the dharma of your lineage?

Siddhartha: Because, Your Majesty, what you speak of is the lineage of Siddhartha Gautama. But I, the Tathagata (Thus Gone One), am now no longer Siddhartha Gautama, but Buddha. And all the former Buddhas who have appeared in my Buddha lineage have all adhered to this very practice of mendicancy.

Shuddhodana: But even if one is to beg for alms, with arrangements for your entire congregation of disciples made directly within the royal palace, ought one come there first, or wander picking up scraps from the alleys and hovels of these untouchables?

Siddhartha: Your Majesty, suppose a physician possesses an excellent remedy for a certain disease; whose house should he visit first? That of one who is healthy and robust, or that of one who is deeply afflicted by that malady?

Shuddhodana: Of course, that of one who is deeply afflicted by that malady!

Siddhartha: Then, Your Majesty, I acted rightly by first going to these humble untouchables rather than coming to the royal palace first. Through great discipline, I have at last discovered the ultimate remedy for dispelling the supreme suffering of all humankind, and these untouchables among humanity are supremely sorrowful! They have no food, no drink, no shelter; alas, there is none left to even lovingly stroke their backs and offer solace! I have seen thousands of Chaturvarni (members of the four varnas) stroking the backs of village dogs with affection. I have seen Traivarnikas (members of the three higher varnas) cradling pet puppies in their hands and caressing them. But the golden children of these poor, wretched untouchables—no one cares for them even at the price of a dog! Their very shadow is considered defiling! I found no other beings in humanity as sorrowful as these suffering creatures, and so I went first to assuage the grief of these most afflicted ones and to show them the path to taste the bliss of moksha (liberation)! What impropriety was there in this, Your Majesty?

Shuddhodana: There is no doubt that your thoughts are exceedingly noble. But is it not improper to accept alms from such folk? Their impurity...

Siddhartha: If you speak of impurity, then, Your Majesty, the impurity within these untouchables is precisely as crimson, pure, or impure as the impurity within us Brahmins (priestly class) and Kshatriyas! This same blood, this same varna (social class), colour, form, qualities—they are all utterly human beings, Your Majesty! When washed, their hands too become clean. If rice is washed with such water, by such hands, and placed upon such fire by them, then rice as pure as your own cooks in the homes of untouchables too. Such pure rice, given with pure intent—I accepted it. If merely by my lovingly stroking their backs, those humble souls experience heavenly joy; then for me not to show such generosity in stroking their backs, would that not be to forfeit my humanity? Your Majesty, by the arrogance of varna, man has become man's dire enemy. Therefore, the Tathagata Buddha determines the worth of individuals solely by their merits, by their character; not by birth. He finds the fallen even among those born Brahmin and Kshatriya, and he finds Brahmins and Kshatriyas even among those born fallen untouchables. The fountain of immortality that Buddha has established allows every thirsty soul to drink the water of life. There, the defilement of varna-arrogance is not considered.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Varsha Ritu Aala Re Rāga: X | Tāla: Y | Chāl: Bahar Aayi Re Original: वर्षा ऋतु आला रे । भूत दया- घन द्रवला । तप्त लोक धाला ।। ध्रु.।। ये द्विज चंडाला । जो तो तपला । पात्र तव तैसे ने । जीवन । जाति नचि दयेला ।। १ ।। Translation: The rainy season has arrived! The cloud of compassion for beings has melted. The parched folk are quenched. (Chorus) Come, Brahmin, Chandala (outcaste), whoever is scorched. Receive life as if you were a vessel. Caste does not determine mercy.

Shuddhodana: You are truly a most extraordinary soul! Blessed is my lineage that you were born of me! Siddhartha, Buddha, you must now come to my royal palace for alms with your disciples at least once. And likewise, you must visit my virtuous daughter-in-law, your sorrowing wife, Queen Yashodhara, at least once.

Siddhartha: As Your Majesty desires!

Buddha begins to walk. All disciples follow him, chanting, "Buddham Sharanam Gacchami, Dharmam Sharanam Gacchami, Sangham Sharanam Gacchami" (I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha).

[End of Scene 5]

docs.title: Scene 6
docs.text:
Sunāsheṭjī's House

Sunāsheṭjī: Mother! Mother! You have left me at last, have you not! (He weeps.)

Women: (Each woman speaking a single sentence) Weep not, Sheṭjī! No ill has befallen her; children, grandchildren, daughters-in-law — fortunate was she, poor soul. This is the way of the world. Weep not! When you weep, we too are moved to tears. Even these little ones begin to cry. (All weep.)

Sunāsheṭ: It was well for her in her old age. But now I have no mother left. Where shall I find such a solace as a mother's presence!

Women: (Each woman speaking a single sentence) Why say so, Sheṭjī? We, your four kinsfolk and neighbours, are here, are we not! We stand in the place of a mother, indeed. We shall not let you feel that your mother is gone. Weep not, Sheṭjī. (They weep.)

Shākambhaṭ: (Entering, aside) Hmm, hmm. I have arrived precisely on time. By having him write this note for me yesterday with his own hand, he is now firmly ensnared in my trap. What does this note say? ‘To Shākambhaṭ: That you should not disclose anywhere the secret concerning my mother and your father, and that I should willingly forgo the debt due to me from you, as was agreed upon between us—according to that understanding, I hereby give this receipt that I have received full payment for all monies owed to me from you.’ He went to entangle me in a written receipt! A merchant's nature is such that once a transaction occurs, he immediately demands 'in writing', and thus he blurted it out and fell into the trap! Too clever by half, and his ox stands idle! Pressing forward, alas, alas! Brother, Mother is gone at last, is she not! If my own mother died, so be it, but now this stepmother too is gone! Oh, how much my father – that is, your father – loved her!

Sunāsheṭ: (Starting up, aside) Is this rogue about to cause some trouble again! (Aloud) Hush, Bhaṭjībuvā! Weep not, let it be. (He places his hand over Shākambhaṭ's mouth.)

Shākambhaṭ: How can I not weep? Do tears come at one's bidding? She was my very own stepmother, was she not! And you are my very own stepbrother, for my father—(Sheṭjī puts his hand over Shākambhaṭ's mouth and silences him)—he is—brother—your—

All People: What is this, Bhaṭjībuvā? Because of grief, must you utter such unseemly words? Consider your caste! Is this a play that you should speak such nonsense?

Shākambhaṭ: It is a play of your grief. Your caste is adopted, but my caste is the true caste of this brother of mine! Now I shall speak everything. (Sheṭjī silences him.)

Sunāsheṭ: Oh, gentlemen, this Brāhmaṇa (Brahmin) is our hereditary Upādhyāya (family priest), raised in our very home. He was like a son to her. Grief has driven him mad. Why heed him? Go, make preparations for the funeral rites. Come, ladies, into the house. Uncles, go to the market. Gather the provisions. What good is mere weeping now? Go! (All depart.)

Shākambhaṭ: Oh, I shall carry my mother's bier. This is my father's letter; this is my brother's letter!

Sunāsheṭ: You wretched Bhaṭūṛyā! If you attempt to extort more money now, I shall hand you over to the king's men! What was agreed upon yesterday?

Shākambhaṭ: This note was agreed upon. In it, you yourself have written that there is some secret concerning your mother, and that I should not reveal it. I shall read this note before these people! Was it not you who, by invoking the charioteer Bāṇa, ruined me? (Loudly) He is my very own stepbrother—

Sunāsheṭ: You have put a noose around my neck, you rogue! Oh, silence! At least tell me once and for all what you will take to keep quiet.

Shākambhaṭ: A thousand, precisely a thousand! (Loudly) Oh, Mother, when your husband passed away in Kashi, my father...

Sunāsheṭ: Oh, silence! What is to be done! Where did I give that rogue the note! Oh, Shākambhaṭ, do not cast doubts into the minds of my kinsmen and leave my mother's corpse lying at the threshold! Have some humanity! Where shall I find a thousand now! Forget everything now; take this salakaḍī (bracelet) and give me that note. People are beginning to arrive, here, give me that note, you rogue, give it quickly, take the salakaḍī, take it, take it, give it!

Shākambhaṭ: (Laughing) How he forces the salakaḍī into my hand! But! He is my very own stepbrother. (They exchange the items.)

Sunāsheṭ: (Seeing the note in his hand) Go, go, do not stand here another moment!

Shākambhaṭ: Oh, I merely stand, Sheṭ! I do not weep, I stand laughing. Merely stand.

Sunāsheṭ: Not merely stand, nor for seasoning! Be off, go! (Shākambhaṭ departs, laughing.) Scoundrel! Village ruffian!! Once my mother's aurdhvadehik (post-funeral rites) are concluded, I shall deal with him, but—

docs.title: Scene 7
docs.text:
(Buddha, his disciples, and Commander Vikram are seated.)

Buddha: Commander Vikramdev, you are the chief of this Shākya Rāshtra (Shākya Nation). You are also a great sage among the Shākyas, and I know that in your youth you attained perfection by meditating on the profound truths of philosophy with a disciplined mind, observing the discipline of yajña (ritual sacrifice), charity, and austerities. Therefore, one of my main objectives in returning to Kapilavastu is to reveal to you, especially among all the Shākya people, the treasury of ārya satya (noble truths) I have discovered, and to secure your cooperation in carrying the momentum of this great dharmachakra pravartan (turning the wheel of dharma) to the ends of the earth, thereby freeing all beings from sorrow. It is my desire, therefore, that you accept the sanyāsa (renunciation) initiation and join this bhikṣusaṅgha (monastic order). Alas, this very world, even heaven, burns in the fire of tṛṣṇā (craving). The wise man must cast it off like vomit. Just as a creature escaped from a forest fire does not re-enter it, and no one desires a disease to return once cured, so too the wise man does not delight in this world again. In such a state, I fail to comprehend how perfected beings such as yourself can remain in this world, and especially in this military profession, so tainted by violence and treachery.

Vikram: How so, Lord? Just as you, the Ender of Sorrows, can remain in this body afflicted by birth, sickness, old age, and death, even after attaining Nirvāṇa (liberation/extinction of desire)! I ask the Tathāgata (epithet for Buddha): Does this physical body, along with that wisdom and the cessation of tṛṣṇā upon the attainment of Nirvāṇa, instantly dissolve, vanish, melt away like a mirage? If not, is it desirable to forcibly destroy it, to commit suicide, to instantly break the shackles of the body? If not, must not even the liberated, even the Buddhas, sustain their bodies? Even if it be videha-mukti (bodiless liberation), if physically it is sadeha (with body) until death, then must not the mundane duties of bodily sustenance be performed? Moreover, great souls like yourself do not wander alone in the forest like a rhinoceros, indulging in the joy of liberation, but rather, moved by the sorrows of the afflicted, you establish this vast enterprise of preaching, propagation, the Saṅgha (Buddhist monastic community) of disciples, debates, monasteries, and abbacy, all to bestow upon the people the benefit of eternal happiness. Why is that?

Buddha: Commander, it is true that the body does not vanish immediately after the attainment of Nirvāṇa. If so, you ask: 'Is it desirable to forcibly abandon the body after Nirvāṇa?' To that, the Tathāgata's clear answer is that forcible abandonment of the body is a new karma (action/deed), and as such, it leads to rebirth. And to transcend birth and death is indeed the Tathāgata's goal. Therefore, the Tathāgata has not abandoned his body. The bodily existence, a consequence of past karma, will cease of its own accord when its time comes! Far from destroying the body, even self-mortification is not sanctioned by the Tathāgata. The Middle Path is the golden path. Keeping the body healthy and efficient and constantly wearing it out in altruistic service for the welfare of the people, this is true bodily austerity. Compassion is the beloved of the liberated, and constantly showering the nectar of Nirvāṇa upon those afflicted by sorrow, motivated by that compassion — this is the renunciant's worldly existence.

Vikram: Then renunciants, too, have a worldly existence! You mentioned the doctrines of rebirth, karma, and the fruits of karma, as other-worldly principles, as reasons for not destroying the body immediately upon liberation. I shall set aside discussion of these as irrelevant to my present purpose. And I desire to discuss only the worldly aims, nature, and consequences of the practical conduct of living out one's bodily existence, or the renunciant's worldly existence inspired by altruism, such as great souls like yourself establish—since even those who have themselves attained Nirvāṇa, who have experienced self-realization and self-grace, deem immediate bodily destruction undesirable. I ask the Tathāgata: Is not the main difference, in your opinion, between the conduct of a liberated one living in a monastery – concerning food, clothing, and sleep – and that of an bound householder, simply that the former acts dispassionately, for subsistence, or for egoless altruism, while the latter does not?

Buddha: Yes.

Vikram: Then, if someone, a wise and perfected one, were to carry out these activities, this worldly journey, with such dispassionate wisdom for the sake of altruism even within a household, then from the perspective of the videha (bodiless) state, there could be no objectionable difference between such a monastic and such a householder, could there?

Buddha: I concede that the conduct of a videha-mukta (bodiless liberated one) can proceed within a household just as within a monastery. Temptations exist even in monasteries! However, it is evident that they will be greater within a household.

Vikram: But that fear applies to aspirants, not to the liberated or perfected ones. For we call him an aspirant who still fears temptations, not a perfected one. Now, since the liberated one undertakes this vast enterprise of propagating the dharma and serving the people solely for altruism, for compassion towards the suffering, the main question I wish to have answered by you is whether this worldly altruism is best achieved by indiscriminately giving sanyāsa-dīkṣā (initiation into renunciation) to all, or by becoming a monastic, or by remaining a householder. Is not the principal distinction between the sanyāsāśrama (stage of renunciation) of a videha and the gṛhasthāśrama (stage of householder) of a videha, or, in short, between householdership and renunciation, that in the sanyāsāśrama one must generally make an absolute renunciation of kāminī (woman/sensual desire), kṛṣi (agriculture), and kṛpāṇa (sword), whereas in the gṛhasthāśrama this is not required? By kṛṣi is meant the livelihood of sustenance, by kāminī procreation, and by kṛpāṇa participation in armed conflict when necessary.

Buddha: Generally, as you say, the renunciant must take a vow of absolute renunciation of kāminī, kṛṣi, and kṛpāṇa; that is indeed the main practical difference between the two āśramas (stages of life).

Vikram: Then, O Tathāgata, I state explicitly that the work of altruism can be accomplished to a greater extent even by the liberated if they adopt the gṛhasthāśrama rather than the sanyāsāśrama. Not only that, but the recruitment you are making to your renunciate bhikṣusaṅgha, without the slightest consideration of suitability, of all those who wish to become a bhikṣu (mendicant monk), will lead to a great disservice in the transformation of beneficence! Yesterday you admitted Rāhula, your own eight- or nine-year-old son, into the bhikṣusaṅgha! Now consider the enormous calamity that will befall by indiscriminately drawing even tender children, who have no notion of what worldly life or renunciation is, into the renunciate bhikṣusaṅgha! Let me take the case of this very Shākya Nation as an example. You embraced renunciation; you gave sanyāsa-dīkṣā to Prince Ānanda and Devadatta; and finally, Prince Rāhula, that eight-year-old child, too, has been taken into the bhikṣusaṅgha, thus plucking the last bud from the vine of the Shākya royal lineage, which is already nearing its demise. With all the best men, even from the feudal clans, having taken sanyāsa, the growth of excellent progeny from virtuous and noble seed has ceased in this nation. Only the progeny of the vicious and inferior people continued to increase. In such a situation, the same misfortune will befall the Shākya race as befalls the crop of a farmer who merely casts aside good seed and sows only rotten, inferior seeds! If your propagation continues in this manner, with the first vow of sanyāsa-dharma (righteous duty of renunciation), the renunciation of kāminī, and celibacy, leading to such depopulation and decline in good progeny, then hundreds of these people will break their ploughs, abandon their looms, leave their shops, and swell the ranks of beggars in the bhikṣusaṅgha, living off the labour of others! For the abandonment of agriculture is the second vow of sanyāsa-dharma! Let others cultivate the land until they die. To eat that ready-made food is not a sin in sanyāsa-dharma. But farming is a sin, for many creatures die by the plough, hence agriculture is violence-prone! The renunciant himself will not engage in such sinful farming — but he will not refrain from eating the food of those sins, perpetrated by others! It would be less sinful for the renunciant to farm himself and eat that food than this hypocrisy.

Buddha: Commander Vikram, are not renunciants like me a kind of farmer? Behold, I clear the wilderness of this worldly illusion and plough the field of the mind with the plough of knowledge. Moral principles are the handle of my plough, industriousness is its ox, I sow the seeds of saddharma (true doctrine) tenets, it is watered by the sight of good deeds, and thereafter it yields a crop of eternal life that ends all sorrow!

Vikram: But, Lord, how many such symbolic farmers like yourself are there in your sanyāsī (renunciant) Saṅgha, who cultivate the nectar-fruit of the supremely auspicious teachings of social virtue? How many are there in this whole world? One, two, at most three. But behold how the economic strength of the nation is weakened by the idleness of the hundreds of unemployed sanyāsī bhikṣu vairāgī (renunciant monks, ascetics, etc.) who gather under the yellow banner of these lone, true farmers! For every person who forsakes worldly life to become a sanyāsī or śramaṇa (ascetic), society loses the earning capacity of two persons – that of the renunciate śramaṇa himself, and that of the worker who supports the śramaṇa. Every śramaṇa is an embodied tax upon every useful profession in society! Take your own Saṅgha! In eight years, thousands of people have joined it. If this continues for a thousand years, that number will reach millions! Furthermore, does not this worldly existence of the renunciant require anything? Though they may not have a double-storied mansion like a householder, they need robes; though not pleasure palaces, they need vihāra (monastic residences); though not temples, they need monasteries; though not modaka (sweets), they need salt and bread. They need sandals, blankets, physicians, medicines, utensils, and even quarrels! Did not the Tathāgata himself often have to threaten to disband the Saṅgha due to the quarrels between opposing factions within it? Lord, just as a household where one brother earns and four merely wander about as idlers is bound to fall into ruin, so too will a society, deprived of the wealth-production of millions and burdened by their upkeep for generations, inevitably fall into ruin. The second vow of sanyāsāśrama, the abandonment of the wealth-producing occupation of agriculture, will have such dire consequences, leading to the misfortune rather than the welfare of the people.

Buddha: But Commander, material wealth is not the only true wealth. Worldly advancement is not the sole puruṣārtha (aim of human life) of man. You forget that other-worldly advancement is the true puruṣārtha!

Vikram: Nay! Nay! You have already conceded that the practice of dharma essential for attaining Nirvāṇa, or for the sake of Nirvāṇa, can be achieved even in the gṛhasthāśrama. Therefore, setting aside other-worldly welfare as a common factor for both, it is the comparison of worldly gains and losses that must be made. Indeed, even for the renunciant's existence, the householder's existence is essential. Only if the householder cultivates rice will the renunciant eat by begging for bhikṣā (alms)! If one possesses a detached mind, is there any difference in being bound by spending time begging or spending time farming? Therefore, I say that even liberated ones like yourself could achieve greater public welfare if, instead of binding yourselves with the distorted vows of sanyāsāśrama, you were to live lives of public service within the natural tradition of gārhasthya (householdership). But even if we set aside the question of such extraordinary beings as the Lord, the entry into sanyāsāśrama must be strictly prohibited for all other people. For the two vows a renunciant must take – the absolute renunciation of kāminī and kṛṣi – lead to the decline of population and wealth in a nation, causing harm, as I have just demonstrated. But far more dreadful damage is being inflicted upon this society, this nation, by the renunciant's third vow, the renunciation of the kṛpāṇa, by that deluded ideal of extreme Ahiṁsā (non-violence)! Lord, this is not extreme Ahiṁsā; this is extreme self-destruction! And since the destruction of the self is also violence, extreme Ahiṁsā thus implies extreme violence! Such is the strange import of this foolish definition of Ahiṁsā.

Buddha: But we are not at all partisans of extreme Ahiṁsā. Not only that, but to resist aggressors with proportionate force and counter-attack for the protection of the righteous and for self-preservation is not violence; on the contrary, it is a meritorious act that thwarts the game of violence. Such is the opinion of the Tathāgata. But this is the duty of the gṛhasthāśrama, not of the sanyāsāśrama!

Vikram: And that is precisely why I say that the sanyāsāśrama, which requires the absolute renunciation of the sword that protects justice, is the greatest calamity that can befall any nation! A nation where millions of people take oaths not to wield the plough, not to touch weapons, and reside in monasteries, is bound to sooner or later cry out for food, become weak, and fall prey to the sharp claws of some worldly, aggressive nation, like a tiger's pounce! By advocating such renunciation-prone ways, the very worldly existence for whose welfare you, even in your state of liberation, undertake this dharmachakra pravartan and this Saṅgha activity, will surely be utterly destroyed. But in the end, this great religious institution of yours, these Saṅghas, these millions of bhikṣus, these spiritual practices, these meditations, these hermitages—this entire renunciate world—will also be torn asunder and annihilated by the bloody talons of cruel wild beasts and even crueler demons!

Buddha: But Commander, a renunciant also holds a kṛpāṇa. A weapon it is. Though it be not of iron, it is for that very reason more efficacious than iron. That renunciant's weapon is called Kṣamā (forgiveness)! Vikram, ‘Kṣamā śastraṁ kare yasya śatrūstasya karoti kim?’ (What can an enemy do to him who holds the sword of forgiveness in his hand?)

Vikram: What? Death! Annihilation of life! Only he who possesses the power to punish can forgive. The forgiveness of the weak, who lack the power to punish, is called surrender—not a weapon! When a cow lies down meekly before a hungry, bloodthirsty tiger, will that tiger spare her, fearing her weapon of forgiveness? Even if that cow says, "I forgive you," the tiger will surely devour her; even if she says, "I surrender," he will devour her! A nation that relies on the foolish hope that continually forgiving wicked enemies will make them cease their aggression will be utterly destroyed by those same enraged enemies, who consider such forgiveness an affront, as soon as an opportunity arises! Such examples have occurred in history, and alas, they are yet to occur! This Shākya Nation of ours is a republic. On one side lies the powerful monarchical state of Kosala, on the other, the monarchical kingdom of Magadha. Between these two powerful monarchical states, the Shākya republic is caught. The moment it becomes even slightly weak, it will inevitably fall prey to the aggression of one of these two vultures. In such a situation, to hold before the people of this nation the distorted ideal that not touching weapons is the excellent way of life, the pinnacle of morality, the sacred path to attaining the Buddha's grace, seems to me utterly self-destructive.

Buddha: That would be true, were it not that I am striving to turn away even the two aggressive monarchs you cited from warfare; indeed, I have all but done so. See here, does it not seem shameful to you that men should butcher men like vegetables with swords merely to establish superiority in a savage struggle for power? Likewise, if all nations of mankind were to resolve to desist from this shameful thirst for war, if all were to practice the supremely generous principles of my dharma — love, compassion, forgiveness, peace, and Ahiṁsā — then would there be any cause for an individual or a single nation to fear? Behold, it has not been even ten years since the Tathāgata established this Saṅgha, and already King Pradyotana of Kosala and King Bimbisāra of Magadha, whose aggression against our Shākya race you so intensely fear, have both taken initiation into the Tathāgata Buddha's dharma and become our disciples! If the most capable men of the Shākya Nation, like Commander Vikram, were not merely to accept my discipleship but actually embrace bhikṣutva (monkhood) and set forth with me to spread this compassionate dharma, then all these nations would place their trust in our teachings; they would no longer truly feel the necessity of war; they would abhor it; and you would become a partner in the great merit of uprooting war entirely from among humankind! Vikram, is not the goal of eradicating war, strife, and bloodshed from the world, a noble enough endeavour for us to exert our utmost efforts and make the ultimate sacrifices?

Vikram: Lord, it is indeed noble, noble in the extreme. But I entertain grave doubts as to whether it is possible, and furthermore, whether it is possible by these means.

Buddha: Commander, regarding that doubt, I say only this: have a little faith! If you will aid me, you shall see the cessation of armed warfare in India within, say, twenty to twenty-five years! You shall witness the era of weapons give way to an era of peace!

Vikram: May God grant that it be so! The most terrible enemy of mankind, the destroyer of men, is man himself; may this stain upon humanity be washed away as soon as possible, and may the honour of establishing the empire of peace be bestowed upon our Shākyasiṁha Tathāgata Buddha alone! However, gentlemen, with great sorrow yet fearlessly, I must voice my apprehension that not only after twenty-five years, but even after twenty-five hundred years from today, the prevalence of the age of weapons will still be manifest in this world, by its ill fortune; might will continue to be right; the triumphant charger of blood-stained empires will rampage across the earth, and under its hooves, those will be crushed first and foremost who, deeming this dream-utterance of an age of peace a prophecy, rely upon it and are the first to renounce arms, becoming so weak as to depend on the mercy of others! They will swallow the noose of violence for the allure of Ahiṁsā! The dire consequences of this terrible delusion, which admits anyone into the sanyāsāśrama and thereby renders millions of people impotent with the vow of renouncing arms, will be suffered by India for twenty-five generations! Nevertheless, lest future generations mistakenly believe that this experiment failed because a peerless soul like Lord Buddha lacked support in this meritorious endeavour, I shall comply with the Tathāgata's wish; and from this day forth, I join this bhikṣusaṅgha. (Removing the kṛpāṇa from his waist) This sword, dedicated to the service of the Shākyas, and my only son, Vallabha, I entrust to the care of my Shākya race, and I embrace the parivrājaka (wandering ascetic) āśrama.

Buddha: Commander, this sacrifice of yours for the welfare of the people is commendable, such that even the gods would nod their heads in approval, exclaiming, "Blessed! Blessed!" Behold, come what may, even if history records that we strove to our utmost to establish an empire of peace, compassion, and love in this world, even if humanity gains experience from the outcome of such an experiment, whether successful or not – even that failure must be deemed partially successful! Come, Shariputra, take this honourable newcomer to the Saṅghārāma (monastery) and administer the Saṅgha-dīkṣā (initiation into the Saṅgha).

Song:

Song Details: Title: Today the Age of Weapons ends Chāl: Rūp Jovan Guṇ Gharau Rahat Hai Original: आज शस्त्रयुग जगी सरतसे । शांतियुग अहा आले ।। ध्रु. ।। दंड हिसकि त्या । दया परतवी । त्याग न वांछी । कलह विझाले ।। १ ।। Translation: Today the age of weapons doth conclude on earth; Behold! The age of peace hath dawned. (Chorus) It snatcheth punishment, and mercy doth restore; Craving it desireth not, and strife is quenched.

(All depart, uttering ‘Buddhaṁ Śaraṇaṁ Gacchāmi, Dhammaṁ Śaraṇaṁ Gacchāmi, Saṅghaṁ Śaraṇaṁ Gacchāmi’ (I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha).)

docs.title: Scene 1
docs.text:
Sunas Shet: (Clapping his hands with joy) She is dead! At last, this Shakambhat's wife is dead. Ever since she fell ill with patki (cholera) yesterday, I have been waiting for her to die! When my mother passed away, this vile Shakambhat concocted a false accusation and caused her corpse to be laid at the doorstep, and now the opportunity has come for me to take my revenge. Now I shall turn his own trick upon him. Fearing that some ill repute might attach to my mother and that my caste might be ostracized even at the funeral pyre itself, I then gave that fellow, the priest, a salkadi (ornament) — now I shall make him disgorge it. Moreover, I shall take his remaining house on mortgage; only then shall I release him. His wife, Kshara, was my bosom friend. I shall simply go about proclaiming that I shall be the one to light her funeral pyre! Oh, Shakambhat, you shall reap what you have sown!

Shakambhat: She is gone at last, this woman! A wife she truly was, who quarrelled her whole life and died. And she died so suddenly that not only others, but even I myself, might suspect if I had poisoned her. A truly chaste wife! I am to receive a sharp lesson for having wedded her, even after her death; so suddenly did she pass. Here come her sundry relatives! The women and folk from the neighbourhood! Not even an hour has passed since her corpse was laid out, and all have gathered. Like flocks of kites and vultures descending upon a beast as soon as it falls, these relatives await who will die when. Indeed, when someone dies in another's house, it is quite a spectacle! If I were to receive an invitation to a pauper's wedding procession and tidings of a rich man's funeral procession simultaneously, I would first go to witness the spectacle of the rich deceased. The bathing of the corpse, the children who watch, alternately fearful and venturing closer, that exhibition of men and women, the weeping by turns, the putrid hideousness of the bare corpse and the embellished hideousness that becomes it after adornment, the filling of the lap (with auspicious items) — after their laps are filled, some women's corpses even appear more radiant than many living women. At least more fair and smiling than our Lanka here! Then, the funeral procession, at times, is filled with more colour than a dindi (pilgrim's procession) on Ekadashi; the blazing of the pyre! When all this spectacle is underway at a house of death, if one receives a call from a living member of one's own household, the mind does not wish to depart, but remains engrossed there — this is an experience common to many. Verily, man is fond of festivals; even if that festival be of death! Leave aside others, but often, even when someone dies in one's own home, what must the minds of the assembled people be thinking, even amidst the genuine surge of grief? Weeping, such thoughts cannot but arise: "Does she truly grieve, or not? Does he look at me, or not? It would be well if such-and-such person were to see me weeping." As for me, I confess, I harbour a peculiar fancy to witness my own corpse! Here they all come! Now the main difficulty is bringing forth tears. If I do not weep copiously today, what will people say? Indeed, just as women weep when their sole husband departs, so too, when a sole wife passes away, we ought to weep. But how is it that tears do not yet come? I feel quite ashamed. As the ritualistic commencement of the funeral rites, I must at least produce a lament.

(Begins to weep, just as the women arrive.)

(Aside) Oh, how strange, as I weep, genuine tears begin to flow!

Women: (Each speaking a sentence in turn) Oh, Bhatjibuwa (priest, an honorific), now you must control your heart, we say. Her soul has turned to gold, yes, she departs with a full lap (of auspiciousness). Oh, what a good nature she had! Peace, Bhatjibuwa, seeing you weep, tears come to us too! These children...

Shakambhat: Women, omit that sentence about children. As a special exception for this occasion, omit that particular sentence from these customary Prakrit (vernacular) pronouncements, just as there are customary Sanskrit hymns for the funeral rites, for she had no children. And then say that one remaining sentence: "Bhatjibuwa, you must restrain your grief, paying heed to the ways of the world." Once one of you utters that, I shall be able to control my sorrow.

(Weeps again.)

Women: (In turns) Bhatjibuwa, you must restrain your grief according to the ways of the world! Indeed, when Sunas Shet's own mother died, we told him, and he controlled his grief. He did not weep so much; and how is it that you lose all patience?

Shakambhat: Women, this very memory of yours makes me weep all the more, my fortitude crumbles! For when Sunas Shet's mother passed away, you ten relatives and neighbouring women, feeling sorrow, said to him, "Though your mother is gone, we are here, are we not? Consider us in place of your mother, we shall care for you likewise!" Then Shetji restrained his grief; but today my wife has died, and so many of you are here, yet no one says, "Shakambhat, it is true one wife has died (weeping) but we many women are here, are we not? Consider any one of us you please in Kshara's stead."

Sunas Shet: (Entering, weeping) Where is my beloved! My Kshara has left me! Oh, let me embrace her one last time!

Shakambhat: (Jumping up suddenly) Hey, you vanagata (low-caste fellow), what do you say?

(Aside) It seems this esteemed gentleman intends to turn my own trick upon me. Truly, the rug has come around my neck! But what use is weeping now? I must face this calamity.

(Aloud) Hmm, hmm, Shetji! Come here.

Sunas Shet: You priestling, now tell me whether I have caught you in a snare or not. Now, when your relatives arrive, I shall make a great commotion. Else, return the salkadi and mortgage your remaining house! And...

Shakambhat: Let that salkadi and such be. Oh, I was mistaken! Forgive me, some humanity...

Sunas Shet: Humanity burnt on my mother's pyre. Hand over the salkadi. — The house on mortgage! See, your caste-folk have arrived, hmm, shall I shout?

(People enter.)

Shakambhat: Hmm. The fellow has mounted his high horse. Come then, shout whatever you wish to shout!

Sunas Shet: (Weeping and shouting) Gentlemen, call me mad! Call me insane! Call me vile – but I am truly mad with grief. Oh Kshara! My friend – my beloved of eight years! How much she loved my nose! We harboured a fervent secret love for each other! Oh, let me embrace her one last time! I shall perform sahagaman (self-immolation) with her corpse! Release me!

People: Bhatji, what is this matter? This fellow smears darkness upon your entire lineage! If this be true, then this is a question of caste!

Shakambhat: It may be a matter of caste. But not of mine; it is a matter of the caste of that dead corpse. What, Sunas! Do you wish to give the corpse a last embrace? To perform sahagaman? Hmm, come then (rolling up his sleeves). Hmm, come, bind him to the bier as well! Bring that corpse!

(The people bring the corpse.)

Sunas Shet: (Startled) Ah! Oh, Bhatjibuwa, why do you come to such an extreme at once! Will you not propose some compromise?

Shakambhat: Fool, how would compromise suit such fervent love as yours! The soul of your beloved will writhe in agony if you do not burn with her! Come, come, bind him to this corpse!

People: Oh, but such corruption within the caste! This corpse! How can this be permitted?

Shakambhat: This corpse, along with him and this bier, shall travel on my shoulders. (He pulls Shetji and presses his face towards the corpse's face.)

Sunas Shet: Oh my goodness, oh, I am filled with terror just by looking at this corpse. If you lay me beside that corpse even for a moment, I shall faint and even die from fright. (Whispering in Shakambhat's ear) Oh, if you give me ten rupees, it is enough, I will leave without saying a word.

Shakambhat: Nonsense. Today, I shall not let you return! You had love, did you not?

Sunas Shet: But you have misinterpreted it entirely! By God's oath, your wife was my upadhyay's (teacher's) wife – my adopted sister-in-law – a sisterly love!

People: He is a rogue, is he not! Bind him. He said he would perform sahagaman with her, did he not? Did you not say earlier that you would perform sahagaman?

Sunas Shet: Oh, that is, to proceed towards the cremation ground with her corpse, accompanied by you all. To go as far as the cremation ground, that was my meaning! Oh my goodness, oh, release me!

Shakambhat: I shall not release you thus! I shall place you upon the pyre with her, then pour cans of oil upon you, then the wood will catch fire and flames will rise, and you will burn brightly like a lamp, your drops of flesh and blood scattering like sputtering seasoning.

Sunas Shet: (Jumping as if scalded with each of his sentences) Oh, I am burnt, I am consumed by fire. My brother, father, my mother, release me! I will listen to whatever you say, release me!

Shakambhat: Then take out this new pair of your salkadi. Beg forgiveness from all these people! Slap yourself once, hold your ears and leave! You try to turn my own trick upon me, do you? Remember this: "Jeno kam teno thay duja kare so gota khay!" (Each to his own trade, another who tries, stumbles and falls!) Go! Go! Oh, your ear has slipped! Hold it and go!

(Curtain)

docs.title: Scene 2
docs.text:
(Sulochana and Vallabh are seated in the palace.)

Sulochana: My Vallabha! I did not speak your name, you see. I say 'Vallabha' in the sense of 'my beloved', 'my dearest'. Otherwise, as your name is also Vallabh, I might be accused of forsaking the modesty of maidens who do not utter their consort's name without an ukhāṇā (riddle or rhyming couplet)! And if this be a fault, then it lies with your parents who bestowed upon you, my playful spouse, a name that steals away a loving adjective from our tongue and places me in such a predicament. Is that not so? So, may I not say 'Vallabha'?

Vallabh: Speak it then, my Sulochana! – But I, too, did not say 'Sulochana' because it is your name, you see! I spoke it as an adjective, in praise of your enchanting eyes. Else you would say I have abandoned the courtesy of a man not uttering his wife’s name without an ukhāṇā! And if there be any fault in that, it lies with your parents, who, by bestowing upon you such beautiful eyes (sulocana) and then naming you Sulochana, have made it impossible for admirers of merit like myself to even attempt to praise your eyes.

Sulochana: Away with you, dear one; you shall not ensnare me by borrowing my own words. It seems men are quite incapable of original, independent wit; else why would they need to steal our 'leftover' jests?

Vallabh: If we perchance steal a jest of yours, you repay yourselves a hundredfold by stealing our hearts. So it is quits, then!

Sulochana: It is for this reason, I perceive, that your attention towards me has now dwindled almost to naught. Truly, Vallabha, since your appointment to the post of Commander-in-Chief of this Shākya (clan/republic) nation, your regard for me has become quite diminished! Since yesterday, I have been observing whether you recall that today marks the first anniversary of our union of love. My dear, has it occurred to you now? As it is the first anniversary of our love-marriage, my lord, I desire to perform Kāmadeva's (the god of love) worship in my heart.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Mlān Kā Mukhpankajabhā Chāl: Mlān Kā Mukhpankajabhā Original: स्वर्ग ज्याने वाचविला । कामदेवा नमन त्याला ।। ध्रु.।। यद्बले स्त्री । विजय झाला । अंबिकेच्या । चरण चाला । वरति संशय नाचवीला । शंभु शंकर नाचवीला ।। १ ।। Translation: To Kāmadeva, who rescued paradise, our obeisance. (Chorus) By whose might, women achieved triumph; They made Ambikā's feet dance, And stirred doubt above, making Shambhu Shankar dance.

Vallabh: But I say, if by the might of Kāmadeva women have become so powerful, then why do they supplicate before us men, like helpless ones, to obtain permission for the worship of that very deity of love?

Sulochana: Because you are now the Commander-in-Chief of the Shākya nation! It is but a matter of courtesy to show some deference to your position as Commander. Moreover, my erstwhile singular sway over your heart no longer remains. Once this resplendent sword (asīlatā) embraces the waist of valorous men, the pull of us women, like tender creepers, slackens before it. Who can say when this sharp rival of mine will seek to undermine me? Thus, I thought it best to consult both of you before indulging my fond desire. So, shall we not then perform Kāmadeva's worship on the auspicious occasion of our love's anniversary?

Vallabh: But dear one, has the anniversary of our love's union truly arrived? What a joyful matter this is! Then how shall the anniversary of our love-marriage be celebrated by merely performing Kāmadeva's arcā (ritualistic worship)? We are well aware of the noble custom that any day in a life of love may be celebrated by performing the arcā of Lord Kāmadeva. But if today is indeed the true anniversary of our union of love, then, my dear Sulochana, it must be celebrated with the fulfillment of desires (dohada). Speak then, what longings (ḍohaḷe) beset my Sulochana? Our love has grown; that which is twofold, my auspicious one, this familial love of ours shall now become threefold!

Sulochana: Do you see the crude jest of men? I do not like such things. If my father-in-law were here today—

Vallabh: He would not even glance at your face! For you know well that your father-in-law is a renowned sanyāsī (ascetic). And sanyāsīs consider even the remembrance of women a sin. So, to speak on their behalf is out of the question.

Sulochana: But my father-in-law could not possibly be such a fanatical sanyāsī. If he were, would he then have such an inveterate love-thief of a son, who sends secret love-letters to an eligible maiden like me through the hands of maidservants, and steals my heart into his own keeping through them? This is my proof!

Vallabh: And here is my proof. (Presenting a letter) Look, this letter from my father—your father-in-law—came to me just today. How delighted I am to see Father’s letter after all these days! Sulochana, it will be nigh on forty years today since my father, General Vikramsingh, the eminent former Commander of this Shākya nation, entered the bhikkhu-sangha (monastic order) at the insistent urging of Lord Buddha. At that time, Sulochana, you have heard, I was but a year and a half or two years old. From that time until now, to my knowledge, only two such letters have come from Father: one, roughly ten years ago, consoling me on the death of my beloved mother, and this second one, congratulating me now.

Sulochana: What is the congratulation for? It seems they have heard the news of our love-marriage! My dear, do tell me truly; my father-in-law is not displeased upon hearing of our union, is he? An ascetic devoted to penance, and moreover, one of Lord Buddha’s bhikkhus, who glare so fiercely at women – the mere mention of a bhikkhu’s name fills us brides with such dread. You presented that letter as proof against me regarding women only in jest, did you not? There is truly nothing adverse in it, is there? Do tell me, dear one, whose congratulations it is!

Vallabh: Mine! Father has congratulated me on the Shākya nation returning to our lineage today the sword of commander-ship which he laid down forty years ago, by appointing me to that very post. Because I married you…

Sulochana: Because of what? Is he angry? Why do you not tell me? He will not be angry. I shall fall at his feet. Let me see that letter! Go. You will not give it? No? (She makes to leave.)

Vallabh: Hey, foolish one, at least listen. Not only is he not angry; but on the contrary, that I am married, and moreover, to a consort like you from the Koliyan clan of the venerable Yashodharā—

Sulochana: That is not so. Show me the letter. Now I have no trust whatsoever in your piecemeal news. You will not show it, will you? Just you see! I shall not ask again.

Vallabh: This seems to be the first dohada, the first longings, of our wedding anniversary. From these combative longings, the son will be quarrelsome, just like his mother. Hey Sulochana—Oh no, I erred! Wait, wait, he will be quarrelsome like his father, then that is settled! Nay, not even that. It will not be a son, but a daughter! Here, take the letter, Sulochana.

Sulochana: Give it here then. We shall read it together, shall we? No, dear one, you must read it yourself. Will you not?

Vallabh: Oh, but yes. (He opens the letter and reads.) —"My son, Vallabha, I have just received news that the citizens of the Shākya Prājaka (republic), the democratic nation of the Shākyas, have bestowed upon you the rank of Commander; concerning this, we heartily congratulate you and your new bride, whose hand you have taken, and whom we already know to be from the illustrious Koliyan lineage. It is commonly understood that ascetics consider the taking of a woman's hand and a sword (kṛpāṇa) to be tāmasī (dark, ignorant), forbidden, at most pardonable, but not commendable; thus, you might feel hesitant, thinking this act of yours would not seem justifiable to your ascetic father. But Vallabha, I find this attainment of both conjugal status and military command not merely justifiable but indeed worthy of congratulation. We are purposefully sending this congratulatory letter of blessing so that you and all other youths of the Shākya nation may know this.”

Sulochana: (Sighing) My lord, my beloved, my spirit has at last settled. How truly compassionate is my aged father-in-law! He has not even fully seen me yet; yet what boundless affection! Well, will you not read further?

Vallabh: But the subsequent part of this letter is exceedingly grave.

Sulochana: Very well, then you should read it with utter unadulterated gravity. (She stands, her face stern.)

Vallabh: That is precisely the difficulty. One might sweeten one's mouth by rinsing it with seawater, but one cannot assume a grave demeanour when standing before women. At least I, for one, cannot help but smile a little upon seeing you.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Brijpat Prabhudeen Chāl: Brijpat Prabhudeen Original: नारी विधि निर्मि मुळी । पिकविण्या हसे ।। ध्रु. ।। नयनि तिखट जाता रडू आवरणे शक्य असे । परि दिसता नारि हसू आवरणे शक्य नसे ।। १ ।। Translation: Woman was fashioned by the Creator solely to evoke smiles. (Chorus) Though sharp pain brings tears, it is possible to restrain weeping; Yet, upon seeing a woman, it is impossible to restrain laughter.

Sulochana: I am, indeed, such a laughable object to you! So, you will not read it in my presence then? Why such reluctance? I am quite eager to hear it now. Will you not listen to me? Am I not your better half?

Vallabh: Then here, take half the letter, torn off, and read your part yourself! Come, Sulochana, I shall not speak thus anymore. Come! Father writes further: "The destruction of the senses is not mastery over the senses. Even an ascetic does not blind himself by plucking out his eyes, nor become mute by cutting out his tongue, nor lose his sense of smell by stitching his nose, nor become crippled by severing his limbs. Why should not the same apply to all bodily and sensory functions? The natural operations of all these senses are equally faultless, necessary for the sustenance of society; hence, it is false that all purity and merit are stored solely in the extreme renunciation of conjugal life. The misconception spreads among people that extraordinary men are considered extraordinary precisely because they become ascetics. But that is not the truth. Great souls like Buddha would have been worthy of extraordinary status and sacred veneration even if they had remained householders. Therefore, Vallabha, fulfil your conjugal dharma (righteous duty) appropriately and without hesitation. May the womb of your consort be blessed with strong and virtuous progeny. May your sword, wielded for the welfare of the people, ever be capable of punishing the wicked! And in this sacrificial life-journey, may the joys of the householder's life not become fetters that merely impede your feet, but rather offerings that bring that sacrifice to fruition! Such a worldly life (saṁsāra) is as sacred as sanyāsa (asceticism), perhaps even more meritorious!" Did you hear how exalted these thoughts are?

Song:

Song Details: Title: Chandā Kamal Bāl Chāl: Chandā Kamal Bāl Original: संसार रति होय । धर्मानुसरणांत । बेडी पदी ना । बलिदान जरि ही ।। ध्रु.।। संसारचि धन्य । संन्याससम पुण्य । तो भोग श्रेयान् । त्यागाहुनीही ।। १ ।। Translation: Worldly pleasure becomes love's delight, When trodden on paths of dharma. No fetters these, but offerings bright, A sacrifice, though it may be. (Chorus) Blessed is this worldly life, As virtuous as renunciation's strife. Its enjoyment is more meritorious, Than any ascetic's sacrifice.

Sulochana: This is what one calls a true renunciant – a true sage! Do you see how liberal are my father-in-law's views? He is a divine man! But Vallabha, to whom does my father-in-law's letter allude at the end, when it mentions the "fetters of worldly pleasures"?

Vallabh: To whom, you ask? To women! Women are indeed the very fetters upon men's feet.

Sulochana: Is that so? Well, my lord, is Lord Buddha not an extraordinary great soul?

Vallabh: What doubt is there in that! But it is precisely because he cast off the fetters of woman from his feet that he was able to become extraordinary.

Sulochana: That is not what I asked you. You need only tell me this: if King Śuddhodana—that is, Buddha's father—had similarly cast off the fetters of Māyādevī, Buddha's mother, from his feet, would your extraordinary Lord Buddha then ever have been known to people? In that case, at least half the merit of the public welfare achieved by Buddha must go to the female sex, which made Buddha's very existence possible. It was because the golden chain of Kaushalyā's love linked itself to Dasharatha's life like an enchanted ray that the advent of Rāmachandra became possible. If Vasudeva had embraced sanyāsa in his childhood, would Krishna then have sprung up like grass in the pastures of Gokula?

Vallabh: But, my dear, this only proves that men should not consider women utterly useless. But does it then prove that women are not the fetters on men's feet in worldly life? If they were not there at all, what harm is there in saying that men might perhaps be happier?

Sulochana: Very well. Let us drop that subject altogether. But my lord, one thing led to another, and so I ask you something else. Do not laugh that I have changed the topic! Since you are now Commander-in-Chief, a doubt has arisen: is it true that there are military prisons even in the army? They say very harsh punishments are meted out there. You should show some clemency, you know.

Vallabh: That is true. But dangerous offenders such as thieves, robbers, and cruel persons must certainly be immediately fettered.

Sulochana: But such demonic, brutal, and vile persons are the only ones to be fettered, are they not? Not good people, just because you take a fancy to it?

Vallabh: Nonsense! How could such injustice occur! Only wicked wrongdoers are fettered.

Sulochana: Then, my beloved, you tell me: seeing that men, too, shackle only the wicked and evil-doers, and not the virtuous; seeing that God, if superior to man, must be even more just—it is surely impossible for Him to be less just; and seeing that you yourself say God has placed women as fetters on men’s feet—does it not follow that men must have been inveterate sinners in a former birth? Else, God would not have placed these fetters on their feet! You yourself just now outlined the rules for whose feet are to be shackled! If men are ready to adorn themselves with a garland upon garland of such epithets—thieves, robbers, wicked, evil-doers, criminals, sinners, aggressors—then we women are also prepared to be called the fetters placed by God upon the feet of such sinners; understood? Fetters, then, let them be fetters. We women are the chains that tame men, like wild elephants of ungoverned, savage nature. It is because we exist that their steps fall rightly upon the path of dharma. Were these fetters absent, these men would gallop unrestrained upon wrong paths, like maddened horses! Have I not won? Oh, oh! The illustrious and valorous Commander of the Shākyas, in the end, has been conquered by a woman!

Vallabh: It is an auspicious sign! On the very anniversary of the day our seed of love began to grow, my consort experiences the longings for a conquest of the quarters (digvijaya); my son will truly become a universal emperor (chakravartī)!

Sulochana: Tut-tut. The matter returns to its original state.

Maidservant: (Entering) Forgive this intrusion upon your solitude. But the Royal Assembly has sent an urgent summons for General Vallabhsingh for a matter of extreme urgency! A messenger awaits outside.

Vallabh: My dear, I must indeed go. That wicked and ambitious King Vidyutgarbha of Kausal had harboured a desire to pick a quarrel with our Shākya nation. However, word came yesterday that he has finally decided to form a treaty of friendship. An important discussion on this must be due. So, bid me farewell.

Sulochana: But wait for a moment! We were to perform Kāmadeva's worship. This garland is nearing completion. Today…

Vallabh: Do you see! Women are indeed fetters upon the feet of duty.

Sulochana: (Placing her hand over his mouth) Enough of that. You should go properly! This is merely a ruse of men to provoke us to contention and achieve their ends. But women are not born criminals, nor men born judges, to have their conduct scrutinised at every turn. Whether woman is a fetter upon duty or its fulfilment will be seen when an equally important occasion arises.

Vallabh: Then for a moment, consider this to be that important occasion, and bid me a smiling farewell.

Sulochana: I shall not bid you a smiling farewell today. Else you will delay your return as much as you please. I shall not give you a smiling farewell; but if you return swiftly after the assembly, in time for the worship, then I shall certainly greet you with a smile, my beloved!

Vallabh: Truly? Then, as soon as my task is done, behold, I shall return swiftly!

Sulochana: Come, or do not come. We shall say naught. How this board for soṅgaṭyā (a dice game) was laid out. I thought we might play a game today! For we have taken a vow of silence.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Mañjula Rasanā Chāl: Mañjula Rasanā Original: जा जा न वचना । बोला । थांबवीत कोणी न आपणा ।। ध्रु.।। कसा पट मांडिला । लव जरी खेळता या पला । त्यात थोरपण उरतेची ना ।। १ ।। Translation: Go, go, say nothing. Speak. None shall stop you. (Chorus) How the board was set. If you play even a moment, No greatness then remains.

Shākambhaṭa: This is nothing short of a rebellion of Buddha that has crept into our capital, into Kapilavastu! It seems he intends to lay this capital waste! When his son first set foot in the capital, his aged father, our King Śuddhodana, passed away. It was at least fortunate that, though a sanyāsī bhikkhu, Buddha did at least cradle his father in his lap! And immediately thereafter, he ploughed over the royal lineage; he himself was a bhikkhu śramaṇa (ascetic), and he made even the eight- or nine-year-old Prince Rāhula a bhikkhu. Devadatta, Ānanda, and his other brothers were all initiated into the bhikkhu-dharma (Buddhist monastic discipline)! Not only that, but this illustrious person—nay, this revered bhikkhu—granted sanyāsa to General Vikramadeva, whose sword had protected this Shākya republic from the wrath and greed of powerful kings like Kausal and Magadha. How did that General Vikramadeva, abandoning his young son, the infant Vallabhadeva, become a sanyāsī and a bhikkhu then? It is beyond comprehension. There is no doubt that Buddha possesses some marvellous power of attraction. Who is it? Tākaṁsiṁha.

Tākaṁsiṁha: (Entering) Shākambhaṭa, now truly this Buddha-mania has reached its peak! Do you hear this? Previously, he initiated his Yashodharā and his mother Mahāprajāpatī—those two royal ladies—into śramaṇatva (asceticism), sanyāsa, and bhikkhuṇī-hood (nunhood). Ah, he made those royal ladies assume the guise of sanyāsīs, truly! He had their heads shaven, gave them saffron or yellow robes of the ascetic colour, and turned them into bhikkhuṇīs! But now, they say, Lord Buddha has begun indiscriminately admitting any woman into the sangha (monastic order) as a bhikkhuṇī.

Shākambhaṭa: And this horde of bhikkhuṇīs, of female ascetics, will dwell with these bhikkhus, these sanyāsīs, in the monasteries and travel together through towns and villages, eh? Done! Clap hands! Ah, when Prince Siddhārtha—the Buddha of today—abandoned Yashodharā, I, and that 'Ag' of ours, she was alive then! She and I had clearly foretold that after a few days of wandering and changing his ways, this fellow would return to seek Yashodharā in one form or another! Not just Yashodharā, but he would establish a 'bhikkhuṇī-quarter' just as there is a 'queen's quarter'! See, it has literally come true. Ah! I truly am a soothsayer; I honestly feel it myself now! Is it for naught that people place such faith in the efficacy of my amulets, charms, and threads? Tākaṁsiṁha, you are a Shākya kṣatriya (warrior caste), of Buddha's own caste. Why do you not also become a bhikkhu and join them? What have you, after all, just like me—no home, no door! No wealth, no wife!

Tākaṁsiṁha: Until today, I feared that bhikkhu-sangha. I thought a bhikkhu was one who begs for alms! One whose days suffer a famine of gold and nights a famine of women; one who possesses neither heavenly wealth nor womanly wealth. The image of some impoverished, emaciated beggar, utterly destitute, wandering from door to door, used to rise before my eyes whenever 'bhikkhu' was mentioned. But now I see the grandeur of royalty on one side; and the grandeur of bhikkuhood on the other. Even the most ordinary bhikkhu among them appears happier than I, well-fed and well-provided for.

Shākambhaṭa: And now, since beautiful flocks of female disciples will be nurtured in those monasteries, these folks will be happier not only well-fed and well-provided for, but even upon rising from sleep, more so than widowers like you and me who have no hope of a second marriage! Ah, let alone widowers. But even if that wife of ours were alive now, her brother-in-law would have become a sanyāsī and had gone to enjoy the pleasures of worldly life for free, in this very sect!

Tākaṁsiṁha: Ah, for you Brāhmaṇas (priestly caste), becoming a bhikkhu is not so difficult. For alms are your original initiation! But we Kṣatriyas, who have enjoyed royal splendour, must naturally feel some shame in adopting this path of begging!

Shākambhaṭa: It is for this reason, I believe, that this sect was founded by Siddhārtha, a Kṣatriya who personally enjoyed royal splendour, rather than by some Brāhmaṇa! Oh, you fool, this sect is a veritable elixir of immortality (mṛtyuñjaya mātrā) for Kṣatriyas! Come to Buddhism; for you hear, do you not, Buddha's disciples proclaiming everywhere its glory, that by it, death is averted. Whether this is true for Brāhmaṇas or not, it is absolutely true for Kṣatriyas. For the death of Brāhmaṇas, like that of crows, occurs by chance, whenever it happens. But Kṣatriyas, like snakes, will encounter death at every turn! A Kṣatriya, no sooner does he emerge, will not rest until he has bitten another, and will not escape without being trampled wherever he is seen. That is why Kṣatriyas are now crowding into this Buddha sect, for once they don the veil of sanyāsa and cast off the dhotī (loincloth) of householdership, the kṛpāṇa at their waist falls away of its own accord. This means they need not face battle again. Whether the King of Kausal marches on the Shākya nation or the King of Magadha, Kṣatriyas formerly had to go to war first if they wished to enjoy royal splendour; but now, having taken initiation into the ascetic bhikkhu-hood of this Buddha sect, they are entirely freed from the vexation of accidental death. The enjoyment of wealth is also found in the monasteries! Thus, this twofold convenience has been arranged for you Kṣatriyas. By taking refuge in Buddha, your death is truly averted. It is not for naught that General Vikramsingh also became a bhikkhu in the past! Tākaṁsiṁha, stop! Look, one locust from that swarm of bhikkhus is coming this way! Let us at least listen to the amusing information he has about his sect. Ah, this is merely that one-eyed beggar from the village of Kṛṣipalī; but why give him any recognition!

Tākaṁsiṁha: But he described the denunciation of the Vedas as a distinct feature of that sangha. You are a Brāhmaṇa…

Shākambhaṭa: Ah, the Vedas have not seen my face, nor have I seen theirs. What is denunciation or praise for a person with whom one has not even a speaking acquaintance! Moreover, Tākaṁsiṁha, it is precisely because I am a Brāhmaṇa that I am also sthitaprajña (of steadfast wisdom). Upon the shield of the amulet-like Bhāgavata mantra (sacred verse) 'tulyanindāstutir maunī' (one who is indifferent to blame or praise, and silent), I repel the assaults of criticism that ever come my way, and no one ever dares to bring upon me the peril of praise. Ah, here comes another locust. Let us have a little more sport.

Second Bhikkhu: (Entering) Buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi, Dhammaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi, Sanghaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi. (I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha.)

Shākambhaṭa: Stop, stop! Before taking refuge in the sangha, I wish to ask a little about the Dharma. But who is this Buddha, who even rides astride the Dharma? You bhikkhus say Brāhmaṇas exalt themselves in the name of Dharma, but this new teacher establishes his own glory right upon the head of Dharma! First Buddha! First pay obeisance to him, and then poor Dharma! Also, we just saw that the denunciation of Brāhmaṇas is also a tenet of your Dharma.

Second Bhikkhu: Nay! Nay! This is quite mistaken. You are in error.

Shākambhaṭa: Perhaps I may be mistaken. For then I was viewing your Dharma with a single, squinting eye. Therefore, I now desire to behold its true nature through your two-eyed vision, as it were.

Second Bhikkhu: O noble sir, Buddha’s discipline is as cool as moonlight (kaumudī). We are not angered by wrathful rejoinders; rather, we seek to quell that anger with the coolness of our humble words. Lord Buddha not only does not denounce Brāhmaṇas, but he holds them in the highest esteem. Among his chief disciples, many prominent ones are from the Brāhmaṇa caste. The Lord says only this: that a virtuous man who observes the vow of benevolence, is free from ego, and is a brahma-vid (knower of Brahman), is a true Brāhmaṇa. The entire universe will continue to honour him, regardless of his birth. The question is of merit, not of the accidental coincidences of birth. Indeed, even those whom the world reviles as untouchables, the compassionate Lord Buddha draws near with respect—honours them! Then, kim punar brāhmaṇāḥ puṇyāḥ bhaktāḥ rājarṣayastathā! (How much more so the virtuous Brāhmaṇas, devotees, and royal sages!) Buddha’s compassion is as deep as the ocean, as vast as the sky! All humanity, seeking liberation from the three kinds of suffering, declare: Buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi, Dhammaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi, Sanghaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi! (He exits.)

Shākambhaṭa: Alas, he did not even stop for alms.

Tākaṁsiṁha: And how profound his thoughts! What leaf are you and I of such a sangha?

Shākambhaṭa: Why so? Come, let us both ponder deeply right now. Let us analyse the benefits of joining this sangha. What is it? Firstly, they say that by joining this sangha, rebirth is averted. We have no concern whatsoever for that. For this birth has already come and gone. And there is no fear of another birth, at least not in this lifetime. What else?

Tākaṁsiṁha: Death is averted! That, however, is an astonishing benefit, is it not?

Shākambhaṭa: Indeed. Kṣatriyas have truly found this escape route from the clutches of death in battle! But does anyone, upon joining this sangha, escape the death that comes in bed? Furthermore, whose death is averted? Only yours and mine, or also that of our enemies? If the death of all humanity, like mine, is averted, then what is so bad about death? I shall become immortal! My enemy will also become immortal! That means our quarrels, fears, jealousies, and fights! This entire host of troubles will also become immortal! Furthermore, consider this: averting death means living forever. But along with that, one needs food and drink! Merely averting death is of no use. Famine, poverty, and toil must also be averted. Yet, even then, it is a dilemma. Alas, if everyone born were to become immortal, there would not even be enough space in this world to live! You and I, our sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, their children, daughters-in-law, their children, daughters-in-law—seventy generations of ancestors, not merely seven, would sit together to dine in one house. Tākaṁsiṁha, clap hands! Their cooking—the great-great-great-grandmother of the seventieth generation would be sitting and cooking as the esteemed mother-in-law! And playing behind her as a child of the house, the great-great-great-granddaughter—I am breathless. Good heavens! Alas, for such a family, mere terms of relation would scarcely suffice. Names would not suffice to call them by, let alone providing food and clothing. Nonsense! If Buddha has truly discovered a way for all humanity to avert death, then consider it that the death of all humanity has occurred. And if death is averted, then the funeral pyre providers, these sellers of wood for cremations, can be considered utterly ruined! Their business would collapse. They would not even sell enough wood to burn themselves. See how clearly these flaws in Buddha's Dharma are visible to me! Stop, shall I found a Dharma myself? Shall I become an Anti-Buddha? Tut-tut, are my thoughts not becoming too grave?

Tākaṁsiṁha: That is why I say, drop that subject. Such a strain is being placed upon my brain that my brain-matter might rupture, bringing upon me today the death that was to be averted tomorrow by joining the Buddha sect. So, we are not going to join that sangha then?

Shākambhaṭa: Nay, nay, why so? For our main aim is not to avert death, but how to live in luxury until death. And upon becoming a bhikkhu and joining the Buddha sangha, there is abundant food, abundant alms, abundant bhikkhuṇīs, and absolutely no toil. One must secure one's livelihood somehow, must one not? And today, this new path of renunciation (nivṛtti) achieves it more effectively than the old path of worldly engagement (pravṛtti). What is pravṛtti? What is nivṛtti? In both, there is still 'वृत्ति' (livelihood). We Brāhmaṇa mendicants practiced pravṛtti, that is, we would openly stretch out our hands and ask for dakṣiṇā (offering); whereas these Buddha bhikkhus practice nivṛtti, that is, saying, "Oh no, no, this worldly life," they withdraw, stretch out their hands, and ask for alms. Thus, livelihood is secured either way! Come, we shall certainly join that sangha.

Tākaṁsiṁha: I shall come too. Once one becomes a bhikkhu, there will be no fear whatsoever of being pressed into service by Yama-rāja (the god of death) as a Kṣatriya in constant battles!

Shākambhaṭa: Come then, say, "Buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi, Dhammaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi," Oh, wait, but Tākaṁsiṁha, is the news you brought, that Buddha has begun admitting bhikkhuṇīs into the sangha, truly correct?

Tākaṁsiṁha: Alas, I swear by the memory of my deceased wife that this news is true. Else, do you think I am some thoughtless householder who would be so eagerly prepared to become a bhikkhu!

Shākambhaṭa: Then utter that remaining vow too: "Sanghaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi."

docs.title: Scene 4
docs.text:
(General Vallabhsingh enters, saluting Emperor Mahanama.)

Vallabh: Victory to His Majesty Mahanama and to the Shākya Prajaka (republic)!

Mahanama: Come, General. A calamity of such magnitude has suddenly descended upon our Shākya nation as you can scarce imagine! This missive proclaims that Vidyutgarbha, the King of Kosala, who until yesterday offered us false assurances of a treaty of friendship, thereby lulling us into a slumber of delusion, has now suddenly assaulted the Shākya nation from two or three directions, advancing like a storm! Approximately forty years ago, King Shuddhodana, the sovereign of this Shākya nation, passed away. His son, Siddhārtha, Bhagavān Buddha, had already become an ascetic even before that. Not only that, but his son Rāhula, his brother Ānanda, his cousin Devadatta, his wife Yashodharā, the Queen Mother, noble chieftains from wealthy clans, and valiant warriors were also initiated into the renunciant Bhikshudharma (monastic dharma), and Buddha led them into his Sangha (monastic community). But the gravest detriment to this Shākya nation was caused by the renunciation of General Vikramsīnh, who, at the fervent insistence of Buddha, laid down the sword of worldly life and embraced the Kaupīna (loincloth of an ascetic) of an ascetic! For Buddha had vowed that if all nations would of their own accord lay down their swords, their weapons, and if all would deem the cruel act of bearing arms as a sin to be repudiated, then war would be eradicated from the face of the earth, and a reign of peace and compassion would prevail everywhere, even within the lifetime of this very generation! Dazzled by this divine spectacle, every active man in this Shākya nation, like Buddha himself, embraced asceticism. This capital became shorn of valour. Valour came to be regarded as sin. The power of enforcement was disdained as an excess! In such a state, our republic, this Prajakasabhā (assembly of the republic), seated us upon the throne of King Shuddhodana. But we too had become disciples of Bhagavān Buddha. Consequently, the strength of arms has been shamefully neglected for forty years! And now we are reaping the bitter fruit of that very neglect.

Vallabh: Fear not, O Shākyas! Even in this war of arms initiated by the foe, we can yet vanquish him. Firstly, let us all entrust the supreme authority of the Shākyas for the duration of this war to some man in whom the Shākya nation reposes the utmost faith in his valour and integrity. For in times of war, it is most advantageous for national power to be singular in hand, singular in centre, and singular in voice, rather than a discordant multiplicity. Therein shall our scattered strengths now unite, and that consolidated might shall yet prove preponderant against the foe. A man whose word the entire Shākya nation shall itself deem as Nirbandhavat (as law).

A Chieftain: Verily, such a man, by our good fortune, yet lives amongst the Shākyas. One at the edge of whose Khadga (sword) even this very Kosala army has trembled, and at whose mere summons this Shākya nation, infused with the ardour of self-reliance, can even today leap into battle—such a man, such a singular man, yet lives! But alas, alas, he has become an ascetic! His name? The aged father of our young General Vallabh, the Pitāmaha Bhīshma of our Shākya nation – our former General Vikramsīnh!

Mahanama: I hold full hope that that very valiant man will yet deliver us from our nation's dire straits. Behold! That is the Khadga of our former General! I still distinctly remember the day General Vikramsīnh, though he deemed weapons to be as supremely sacred and as essential a means for the sustenance of the people as Shāstra (scripture/knowledge), nonetheless laid down that Khadga for the earnest insistence of Bhagavān Buddha and accepted the renounced Bhikshu's vow. From that day, this Shākya Rāstrasabhā (national assembly) has revered that Khadga in this hall like a deity, to commemorate its gratitude. By the aid of this Khadga, Vikramsīnh had scattered our national enemies ten times over! This Khadga is the incarnate inspiration of our nation. I say, O Sāmant (feudal lord) and Sabhyaho (honourable members), in this perilous hour, let us appoint General Vikramsīnh as our Sarvādhikārī (supreme commander), and the message we dispatch to recall him should be sent through the hands of this very Dūta (messenger)! No human tongue can express our Hṛdgat (heartfelt sentiment) in such eloquent terms as this iron tongue of the Khadga can convey it in its poignant voice. To General Vikramsīnh, the language of this Khadga’s iron tongue will surely seem more familiar, authentic, indispensable, and revered. It is for this very reason that we shall now dispatch this Khadga to him, along with a Rājamudrānkit (royal seal-affixed) invitation, as our messenger! He is an ascetic; he will most probably not touch weapons. Alas, alas, though all this be true, yet he will surely not fail to render some aid. If he but delivers an inspiring message to the Shākyas, and says, "Fight!" then that one word, issuing from his lips, shall make the power of our national Tūṇīra (quiver) unconquerable, like a divine Brahmāstra (divine, irresistible weapon)! The blessings of Bhagavān Buddha and the command, guidance, troops, and leadership of Vikramsīnh—even such indirect assistance must be afforded to the Shākya nation by this Shākya Dhurandhara (leader/pillar) at this time! And it shall be. For they are both offspring of this very Shākya nation. They have suckled her milk from the bosom of this very Bhūmātā (Mother Earth). They must surely possess gratitude for their mother's milk. Furthermore, one reason for this fearsome assault upon the Shākya nation is that Vidyutgarbha, being an implacable foe of Buddha, envies the very lineage of Buddha and desires to lay it waste! Who is it? Messenger, what is it?

Dūta: (Entering) Forgive me, Your Majesty? Four Yojanās (ancient unit of distance) hence from the capital, great confusion reigns in our main Senāshivira (military camp). Vidyutgarbha's army has occupied half the kingdom and is swiftly advancing. Whosoever Shākya comes their way, Kosala soldiers are mercilessly cutting them down. Many villages are burning to the ground. Women and children are being indiscriminately subjected to Shākā (slaughter). There is great lamentation. Throngs of terrified people are fleeing for their lives towards the capital. Upon hearing these dreadful tidings, the courage of this military camp failed. When we recently went to villages for recruiting for the army, people openly condemned us, saying it is a sin to fight, that we shall not bear arms, and that the occupation of a soldier and that of a butcher are equally contemptible. Yet, those who, with great difficulty, joined the army were all faint-hearted. Upon hearing these horrific reports, when they were commanded to advance, they openly broke ranks and retreated from the military camp. When we tried to push them forward, a great uproar ensued. If order is not restored this very day...

Vallabh: Not this very day, but this very Ghaṭakes (instant)! Come, I shall proceed thither with this advancing force. Your Majesty, in our Nagaragṛha (city hall), in that Santhāgāra (assembly hall) of ours, let the Sankata Ghanṭā (alarm bell) sound! Summon all citizens, appoint a Sarvādhikārī (supreme commander), make them fully aware of the Rāshtrīya Sankata (national crisis), and raise a Nāgarik Senya (citizen army). Until General Vikramsīnh's message arrives, I shall organise the army and continue to confront the foe. Our endeavour; success to God! Men and women, householders and ascetics, all who are of the Shākya seed, take up arms! This is the oath of this Shākya race, of this Prajaka — of this nation! Arise! I go now. I am the son of the renowned former General Vikramsīnh of the Shākya nation; I am the present General of the Shākya nation! I shall make the foe realise this henceforward, then only shall I bear the name Vallabhsingh!

(He exits.)

([Curtain])

docs.title: Scene 5
docs.text:
(As she strings a garland, Sulochana hums the following song:)

Song:
