Sulochana: It is indeed so. But this reaction of suppressed anger is the goad to the elephant of madness. If one steps on a snake's tail, the snake quickly turns and bites, and as we die, we render the enemy mortally wounded, not for victory, but for revenge. And because mankind fears that the snake's species is vengeful, people do not dare to crush a snake as easily as children crush an ant or a lizard. An arrow-wounded tiger, even when dying, leaps with this desperate reaction and sinks its teeth into the hunter’s throat. The tiger dies; yet, seeing this vengeful reactive nature of the tiger, no man goes tiger hunting as casually for fun as he would go rabbit hunting. What is an ant! When it bites a man’s foot, it knows full well that by this bite it will not personally survive. But it bites not to live, but to ensure that the one who killed it must suffer some punishment. That biting ant dies. But then, not only man but even snakes rarely enter a nest of such biting ants of its kind! There is a species of bees. As soon as their hive is destroyed, they abandon the pursuit of honey, caring not what becomes of their other bees. Instead, each individual bee will relentlessly pursue the person who destroyed the hive, stinging them. So firmly does its stinger embed itself in the person's body that it cannot retreat. It dies there. Yet, it knowingly goes to die thus. For the satisfaction of dying in revenge gives it greater joy than the satisfaction of a humiliated life. Consequently, mankind never fears an entire colony of silkworms as much as it fears a single one of those bees. This sting of revenge that nature has placed in the anger of all creatures has such a divine purpose: that this tendency for revenge does not let an aggressive assault and its sinful plunder go completely uncostly. Thus, the aggressor does not rush to commit such acts with the same fearless speed as he would if there were no fear of revenge. The rest of the world remains safer from aggressive torment to that extent. Therefore, if the Shakya nation’s death is now inevitable, then not for its own life, but at least for the rest of the world to live, the Shakyas should fall upon Vidyutgarbha like tigers. Each Shakya should die, exacting revenge and meting out punishment, crying out, at least five cruel Kosalas, so that this Vidyutgarbha will not dare to launch such an armed raid on other small, similar principalities in the future. He will not be able to achieve victory so easily! At such a time, revenge is not merely an innate reaction, but a benevolent duty. Therefore, my answer to your question is unequivocally one: Not surrender, but revenge!

Vikram: O young warrior, I offer this caution not to obstruct your decision, but that there may be no diminishment in the heroic and spontaneous reasoning with which you have supported that decision. You have, considering all other causes and effects, omitted one crucial thing entirely. We do not lay down arms. Our answer is not surrender. Revenge! The moment the sound of your decision reaches the ears of that wicked Vidyutgarbha, his sword, too, will fall upon Vallabha’s neck with the terrible impact of its echo, and his head will be severed instantly! You have not forgotten this, have you? It is a different matter if you attach no importance whatsoever to that single consequence.

Sulochana: Who counts an individual in the consideration of the eternal gains and losses of nations! Patriarch, I cannot make the mistake of considering that thought.

First Commander: What understanding or misunderstanding can such an unknown youth have! How can he comprehend the importance of Commander Vallabha! You are a warrior, but you are an ignorant youth, unacquainted with statecraft, dwelling in some village. O brave youth, have you ever even seen that steadfast Commander Vallabha? Ah, if you had seen his charming, divine countenance, alas, at the very word of your decision, your mind's eye would have seen that radiant countenance severed by the wicked Vidyutgarbha’s axe and falling to the ground, and you would have fainted. Who counts an individual? But a nation is not some independent entity floating in the sky! The nation of an individual, and especially an individual like Commander Vallabha, marked by extraordinary personal greatness and vested with the authority of national commandership, is a manifest expression of the nation itself! One of these two lineages, whose history is the history of the Shakyas over the last three centuries, is our royal lineage; it was severed and rendered extinct by the ascetic tongue of Bhagawan Buddha. This second national lineage, next to the royal lineage, is the ancestral line of these Patriarchs. That lineage is being severed and rendered extinct today by your warlike tongue. Alas, alas, and behold Vallabha's young new bride, Sulochana! Maharaj, she is my niece. I saw her when she was a child. She shone like a star! Later, we went far away, and she never met me again. She has not yet even passed her twentieth year. Not even a full year may have passed since her love-marriage! Before the first bloom of flowers has even appeared on her vine of youth, how dare you try to wipe away the tender vermilion of her hopes of happiness! Do not sever the throat of that delicate-hearted maiden with a hair! Young man, do you have any beloved person in this world for whom your soul yearns when you do not meet them? If so, bring that beloved image before your eyes. Then immediately envision the gruesome scene where that beloved person’s dear countenance is sharply severed from the neck by a butcher’s axe, and thick gouts of blood spurt forth; and then remember that the anguish that will overcome your heart with the imagined pain of that scene will be a hundredfold less than the agony Vallabha's beloved new bride, Sulochana, will experience upon hearing the news of his actual beheading, and then speak! What more can I say than this?

Sulochana: I said earlier that in matters of national or global welfare, the question of individual joy and sorrow is secondary. But if you insist on my opinion even on that secondary question, then I ask, even if we lay down arms and the enemy perhaps spares Vallabha’s life, for what purpose would he spare him? When that Vidyutgarbha returns to Kosala after annihilating this Shakya nation, will it not be to parade Vallabha as the conquered commander of the Shakyas before his victorious chariot? To display him as one would a defanged tiger among women and children? It seems to me that such a death in martyrdom would be more desirable to the honorable Commander Vallabha than such a miserable existence. Commander, I, too, have a beloved person in this world still (sobbing, bewildered, to himself) — Oh, what have I said? My mind has revolted! It tries to escape its prison! Reason, you guards, seize it!

Vikram: That is to say, that is to say! Brave youth, why are you faltering! Be firm and clearly state what your heart feels!

Sulochana: (Composing himself) Maharaj, forgive me! My speech wavered slightly. You ask what my mind says! But just as kings imprison internal rebels before entering the battlefield, so too has my intellect imprisoned my mind and sealed its mouth, placing reason as a strong guard. Therefore, my mind has no opinion now; I have an opinion, and I, as a soldier of the Shakya nation, am clearly stating it: rather than branding the life, nay, the very memory of the nation with the eternal stigma of cowardly surrender for the sake of one Commander Vallabha’s life, it is fitting that the lives of Vallabha and all of us be sacrificed in fierce combat, utterly destroying the enemy. My conviction is that Vallabha himself is the son of the Patriarch, a brave man by nature, the commander of the Shakyas, and the beloved of a brave woman! I consent to his beheading precisely because if we surrender and Vallabha perchance escapes, that commander himself would not spare us from beheading ourselves for having feared his beheading. Not surrender, but war—that is my final word?

Vikram: Excellent! Excellent!! O young householder warrior, you have truly made us old ascetic sages bow our heads in shame at your self-control! Indeed, what ascetic could be more self-controlled, more detached, more unblemished than the householder warrior who casts away his own head, as one casually throws a ball of rags, for the sake of his dharma (righteous duty), for his nation, for benevolent justice! Listen, commanders, listen to the final word of this war council! If this young commander had consented to surrender, two votes would have fallen on that side, and that would have become the decisive majority. But since his final word is war, and one has not given an opinion, with one vote each on both sides, the final decision rests upon my heart. Therefore, I render that decision thus: in accordance with the last word of this young warrior, the last word of the Shakyas shall also be: Not surrender, but war! Come, let our army, which has been fighting continuously for four days, rest until tomorrow morning, and tomorrow, fall upon the enemy as a thunderbolt from the sky. Go forth, uttering the last word of the Shakyas. Dismiss this war council!

All: Not surrender, but war! Not surrender, but war! To die fighting!

docs.title: Scene 5
docs.text:
(Sulochana and Nalini, disguised as men.)

Sulochana: (Looking hither and thither) Nalini, look, do stains of blood appear upon my heart? I have committed a heinous murder and am come away!

Nalini: What mean you, my lady! For three days past, returning from the battlefield, you have been bathed in the blood of the nation's foes! The garments upon the breast of such a supremely valorous, warring virangana (heroine) must indeed be dyed crimson with the blood of her adversaries.

Sulochana: Nay, not the garments upon my breast! Behold the heart within my breast! Daily, whilst hewing down the savage hosts of the nation's enemy, Vidyudgarbha, the spurting blood would dye my breast-garments crimson; yet no single stain thereof did fall upon the pristine purity of my heart. But today, today, Nalini, I have come away after the murder of one utterly innocent and blameless. Not the covert or overt slaying of a villain, but the secret murder of a virtuous one, of him who rested his head trustingly upon my lap! The stains of that blood, I feel, have splashed upon my heart! The mere remembrance of that dreadful murder fills me with the dread that some assassin pursues me. Hence, I declare, I must obliterate every trace of this killing. So look, pray look, have any such stains of innocent blood splattered upon my heart! Ah, how can you see my heart merely from without? Peer through my eyes, then shall you perceive my heart. They say the stains of treacherous murder fall upon the heart; and furthermore, my friend, that spilled blood was the blood of one devoted.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Alas, my friend, alas Tāla: | Chāl: Bol Bhavenda Bol Original: हाय सखे गे हाय । सांडी मी जे । अनुरक्ताचे । रक्त ते एक्या ।। ध्रु. ।। मांडीवरी माझ्या । निजवी ज्या चुंबुनी । मी केसाने कापी । कंठा त्याच्या । अनुरक्ताचे । रक्त ते एका ।। १ ।। Translation: Alas, my friend, alas! That blood I spilled, It was the blood of one devoted. (Chorus) Upon my lap he slept, by me oft kissed, His throat I severed with a lock of hair; It was the blood of one devoted.

Nalini: Sulochana, my lady! What words are these you utter! Whose murder? Who is this devoted one? Virangana, why are you thus suddenly distraught? I am filled with fear. Pray tell me clearly what has transpired!

Sulochana: Know you not who is devoted? Nay, he upon whom I was devoted, and who was devoted unto me, he was my beloved! Nalini, I have come away after slaying my beloved. Not by sword. Ah, for such treachery, the sword's edge proves blunt. Behold the sharpness of my tongue! The blow of betrayal, which makes the blade of a sword tremble, was struck by the sharpness of this tongue. Nalini, with my tongue I severed the head of my beloved; with my hair, I cut the throat of my darling.

(Trembling, she sinks onto the couch.)

Nalini: What ominous words speak you, my lady! Has she not suffered a fit of vapours? What shall I do now, my lady? Sir, Sir, should anyone swiftly arrive at our camp, will not this disguise of ours be revealed by such behaviour?

Sulochana: Verily, am I not still in disguise? Then this forgetful conduct of mine becomes truly ludicrous, like some uncultivated actor who, whilst the play proceeds, spies a friend among the audience from the stage and instantly calls out to him, still in his theatrical costume. Therefore, do this now: remove this my dramatic guise. But you, remain in your male attire and stand guard at the outpost of our camp, whilst I retire to the inner chamber and converse with my mind for a while. From the moment we set forth in male guise, I had imprisoned my frail heart and sealed its lips, vowing that they would open only when my beloved's hand should unseal them. But now, that vow have I myself rendered impossible. For, Nalini, it was not merely because I gave an unfavourable opinion that surrender to the enemy was not decided; and if the Shakyas will not surrender, then the cruel Vidyudgarbha has issued an order for my beloved to be slain. This night is for rest; tomorrow, the final assault upon the enemy. Our battle-plan must now be in his hands — and with that, the sword in his hands will be at my beloved's throat! Alas, alas! How shall I ever meet my beloved now! How shall he come to speak and hear the secrets of my heart! The whole world remains to hear my reasonings. Those reasonings I have spoken these past eight days. But now, in solitude, there is none save my own mind to speak to regarding the matters of my heart. Therefore, I shall now for a short while remove the seal from its lips. For a short while, I shall be myself! The remaining acts of my play are ended. Only the final act now remains. Just as actors, having recited the dramatist's lines, spend the interval between two acts backstage as themselves, speaking their own thoughts, so shall I. I shall now cease merely reciting speeches devoid of the sentiment of heroism (veerarasa), and for a moment shall commune with my own mind in my unfettered speech. Yes, solitude. A solitude achieved by the demise of that one, unparalleled soul, my life's companion. Come, let us go into this inner chamber, and shed this theatrical guise. And then, go and sit on guard.

(Both go inside. The inner curtain opens.)

Sulochana: (In woman's attire before a mirror) Hm, hm. Now I recognise myself. This is that same Sulochana. Exactly as she appeared some eight or ten days past, stringing a garland for the worship of Kamadeva (god of love) with her hands, singing the garland-song with her lips, and waiting in her heart for her beloved—waiting for her beloved who had gone forth promising to return immediately—whilst in the innocent solitude of her bed-chamber within her abode! Considering what transpired thereafter as though it had never been, now, Come, my heart, come, and speak with me. That mother-in-law of your discernment sleeps for a moment. So until then, my heart, speak with me to your heart's content. After a day's household duties are done, when the mother-in-law bids the virtuous daughter-in-law go to the temple for an hour in the evening and take some rest, then does she sit and converse with a free heart, laughing. The day of my life is setting, evening is drawing nigh. So come, my heart, let us go to the temple standing. (Taking out a portrait of her beloved) Behold the image of my deity! My god, my beloved, my dearest, pray cling to my breast for a moment thus.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Even today, as I depart Tāla: | Chāl: Khwaja Ke Kadam Pe Original: येचि आजि जाता जाता । एकदा मला घे । जिवलगा मला घे । ये ना । छातिशी मला घे ।। ध्रु. ।। नसे आयुष्य वा धनी ना मृत्युही ज्याच्या ।। प्रिया एकान्त हा ऐका एका तुझा माझा ।। जिवलगा मला घे ।। Translation: Even today, as I depart, Pray take me once into thine arms, My life's companion, take me to thy breast. (Chorus) Not life, nor death's dominion, but This solace, my love, only thine and mine, My life's companion, take me to thy breast.

Ah, how light-hearted I feel, thus conversing so naturally with my beloved in solitude after so many days! You were to return swiftly, were you not? It was the first anniversary of our festival of love, was it not, for our marriage of affection? And for that auspicious occasion, a worship of the propitious Kamadeva was to be performed, was it not? Then why did you not come quickly? I shall not now make the mistake of wasting time in baseless sulking. I shall not even observe a lover's quarrel. At most, I shall but ask: Beloved, tell me now once more, is woman a man's chain or his inspiration? In the battle where you vanquished the savage foe, your beloved, this darling of yours, also vanquished that foe in that very battle. Ere your sword could fall, she snatched it up and did not even let the foe perceive that your sword had dropped. Then, brave warrior, does not this virangana befit you? Then tell me, is woman a man's chain or his inspiration? A man's deficiency or his fulfillment? I know what answer you will give to corner me again; you will say, "True; but who is your guru? Whose disciple are you?" Thine own, beloved, thine own! You yourself taught me these four simple tenets of valour and the science of what is righteous and unrighteous; and this boon of questioning right from wrong, given by you, O innocent Shiva, like Bhasmasura, finally turned against your own life. And in the council of war just now, it became a destructive hand placed upon your own head. Not the destruction of the senses, but their conquest, lies in being ready instantly to sacrifice personal pleasures for the public good, even whilst enjoying sense-gratifications as desired, should they impede its achievement. He who practises such a yoga of action, though a householder, is like a sanyasi (renouncer) and eligible for videhamukti (liberation from the body). These tenets of dharma (righteous duty), of your father, your grandfather Vikramasimha, that military sanyasi, you adopted as your creed and made me adopt as mine; as you taught them, so I practised them. If there was any error in them, the responsibility, O General, lies in your military discipline. For in that council of war, it was not I who rendered that dire decision, but a national soldier of the Shakyas, tempered in the closest instruction and discipline of General Vallabha. But now, I am Sulochana. I am the impulsive, youthful beloved of my Vallabha. O Lord Kamadeva, I was stringing flowers for your worship when you departed! Alas, alas, how withered they are! What is their fault! In this mortal world, flowers shall indeed wither, petals shall fall, fragrance shall vanish. But therefore, I do not go about blaming the world, nor constantly loathing it. For flowers also blossom in this world, petals emerge in this world, and fragrance too pervades this world!

Song:

Song Details: Title: Though they wither in this world Tāla: | Chāl: Maun Man Ko Fasiya Original: सुकतातचि जगि या । जरी की । फुले गळत पाकळी पाकळी । उमलति ना त्याही कलिका । ज्या ।। ध्रु. ।। परंतु सुंदर कळ्या पाकळ्या फुलती ही जगि या । विसर ना हे वैतागीं । तुझिया ।। १ ।। Translation: Though they wither in this world, and fall, Petal by petal, never to blossom again, Those very buds, those fragile petals! (Chorus) Yet beauteous buds and petals bloom in this world, Forget not this, in thy vexation.

My only mistake was that as soon as the flowers had blossomed, I did not swiftly fulfill their cherished desires, adorn them, or offer them in worship as floral tributes. On that day, as he departed, without wasting time in loving silence, I did not swiftly string this fresh garland and place it about his neck! And I did not say, "Pray take me once!" But even now, there is a slight opportunity to place this garland of my devotion about my god's neck! For those who say that there is a heaven also say that those slain in a righteous war, waged for the destruction of villains, ascend to that heaven. So, if that be possible, my beloved, slain, may have gone to heaven and become a god. On the night of battle, I too shall be slain, facing the field of sacrifice, and shall follow in my beloved's footsteps to heaven. Therefore, though this garland be withered, I must keep it with me thus. For if our earthly bodies attain divine status in heaven, why should not the earthly flowers that were with us also attain the status of divine flowers in heaven? Once this remaining night has passed, tomorrow at this very hour of night, as I set foot at the gates of heaven, my beloved will be a god, I a divine nymph, and this garland of divine flowers, a garland of parijata (celestial flower)! My incomplete worship of Kamadeva will be fulfilled. As soon as I see my beloved, I shall place this garland about his neck thus. I shall say, "Pray take me once!" And he will extend his arms and draw me to his vast breast. I shall rest my hands upon those strong shoulders, close my eyes upon his heart thus, and become absorbed in a trance of love.

(At that moment, Vallabha enters and stands within her outstretched arms.)

Vallabha: Sulochana, my friend!

Sulochana: Vallabha? Amazing! They say that when a devotee's meditation reaches its peak, he beholds his chosen deity in person—and it is not false! Am I in heaven or in a dream? My God, are you merely an illusion of my mind? Let it be so! He whom I deemed real vanished like an illusion; then if he whom I deem an illusion shall remain embodied and palpable thus, then that illusion is reality, illusion is truth, truth is illusion. Then, Vallabha, tell me, are you an illusion or a manifestation, or truly present? Are we on earth, in heaven, or in a dream?

Vallabha: My dear, I am truly Vallabha himself. In the end, I am as real in this world of illusion, yours and mine, as I seemed before. I myself doubt whether this is my rebirth or my very birth! But let all that pass, birth or rebirth, heaven or dream, illusion or reality—in this wondrous eddy of a moment, our astonishing meeting has indeed occurred. So come, let us both plunge into this ocean of joy of embrace and be utterly submerged.

(They embrace.)

Vallabha: Sulochana!

Sulochana: Vallabha!

Vallabha: Even if my head were severed, I would not worry. But you gave the opinion that it is not well to surrender to a wicked foe, is that true?

Sulochana: Yes, my dear.

Vallabha: Then I am greatly angered by that.

Sulochana: Nay, my dear, that is impossible. Well, is it true that on that day, you departed for the royal assembly saying you would soon return, and as soon as the war-horn of national battle was sounded, you left me thus, without even a farewell, and became estranged as ever?

Vallabha: Yes, my dear, a warrior's duty permits no retreat.

Sulochana: Then I am greatly angered by that.

Vallabha: Nay, my dear, that is impossible. You are a virangana.

Sulochana: Likewise, it is impossible for you to be angered by my opinion that the Shakyas should not surrender. For, Vallabha, you are the foremost of warriors! But, my friend, my mind is still confused as to whether you or I, or both of us, are merely dreaming. So tell me, by what coincidence are we meeting thus? How were you freed, and how did you know I was here? Pray tell me swiftly, for though I would rather forget myself by lying silently upon your breast in your embrace for this fleeting moment, which is like the fruit of infinite merit, than hear it in detail, yet I do wish to hear a little.

Vallabha: After I was wounded and fell into enemy hands, in the past four or five days, your valour caused the Shakya forces to annihilate Vidyudgarbha's army, which greatly disordered and frightened the Kosala army. Both guards over me were wounded soldiers themselves; they would often drift into unconsciousness. One night, a Shakya farmer from a neighbouring village, whom the enemy forces had forcibly conscripted, by chance stood there; he recognised me and, displaying utmost daring, used his keys to unlock my prison whilst the guards were in their stupor, and led me out. In the disguise of one of his labourers, I escaped from Vidyudgarbha's army. I reached our army thus, and learned of the resolution of the council of war from General Father Vikramasimha. In it, it was decreed that to behold the embodiment of their pride and valour, that young commander who had scorned surrender and had not allowed that stain to attach itself to the memory of the Shakya nation, I should come to your tent. The guard standing outside, instead of challenging me, became flustered and instantly prostrated himself at my feet; I lifted his head and looked, and it was Nalini! In a few sentences she told me what had transpired, and I understood that the embodiment of Shakya valour was this my impulsive, sulking, loving, youthful Sulochana! Now, in tomorrow's final calamity of battle, we shall not be generals. We are merely soldiers in the ranks of this my tiny commander!

Sulochana: Tomorrow's is for tomorrow. Yesterday's for yesterday. My friend, let me remember only this fragment that has been found today amidst that final tomorrow and that harsh predicament; I remember only my Vallabha and myself, his Sulochana, dissolving, melting, and forgetting myself in his embrace thus. My friend, I feel strange. Your departure that day, and your arrival today, both are accidental, sudden, both unbearable; Vallabha, pray take me in your lap for a moment. Let this withered garland of Kamadeva's worship lie about my neck thus. Let me for a moment wave this lamp that has cooled in my eyes over you. My lord, a profound slumber is overcoming me. On this sweet stupor of this last night of my love's final union, O Lord Kamadeva, let the final curtain of my life also fall! But wait; only for tomorrow's battle must you awaken me. I have yet to fulfill my remaining desire to share a couch with you, akin to a bed of battle. So do awaken me just for that. Otherwise, even the final profound slumber of my life upon this bed of love might be disturbed by the suddenness of tomorrow's bed of battle! My lord, my lord, where are you?

Vallabha: What? Sulochana, Sulochana, I am right here. What, what?

Sulochana: I feel a strange, unbearable suffocation. This sweet stupor! Or an enchanting swoon!! Or a sweet demise!!!

Vallabha: What means this! My beloved has swooned whilst speaking! Her pulse, this thread of her life—nay, nay, O innocent love, O foolish mind, this is no swoon. The hand of death steadily pulls and wraps this thread of my lovely beloved's life. O Death, with this thread of her pulse, this thread of her life, you seek to drag her away; but I shall not permit you. Your noose fell about my neck when I was captured by my enemy; but did you, enraged by my escape, pursue me hither? If so, your aim is missed. My throat is my beloved's; a frail woman's throat. Like some unskilled archer, withdraw your errant noose from her throat and cast it about mine! Alas, alas, she is departing! My beloved is being violently pulled away from this my miserly embrace into the snares of death! What shall I do now? Her breath, her life, my treasure of gems is no more! I shall not allow it to leave this repository of her beauty, her body. Upon the captivating face of this beautiful golden casket, like a staunch miser, I shall place this lock of kisses, and I shall not permit the priceless treasure of her life, the gems within her heart, to escape! Sulochana, my darling—what shall I do now! Nalini, Nalini!

Nalini: (Entering) Master, what is this? Why are you suddenly overcome with grief?

Vallabha: My Sulochana has suddenly slipped down the treacherous slope of unconsciousness into the abyss of death.

Nalini: My Lord, what ominous words you speak! How did this happen?

Vallabha: Oh, how, you ask? A while ago, in the council of war, she consented to my demise, did she not? In revenge for that, I, this wretch, her beloved, have slain this his beautiful beloved by plunging the dagger of joy into her heart! Do you not understand? Nalini, when I suddenly departed for the battlefield's jaws of death, leaving her alone, I wounded her with the unbearable sorrow of that accidental separation; and now, upon my sudden return from those jaws of death, I have slain her with the unbearable joy of this accidental union. Nalini, grief cannot be contained within my heart. Breaking the discipline of this military camp, my silent grief yearns to burst forth in a lament!

Nalini: (Listening) What is this? A great clamour is rising somewhere.

Vallabha: Nay, not a clamour—it is the echo of my silent grief, raging wantonly yonder, beyond the bounds of the camp's discipline!

Song:

Song Details: Title: My silent grief Tāla: | Chāl: Kon Khele Tose Original: मूक शोक भर माझा । गे हा हाय । हंबरडा फोडी ॥ ध्रु. ॥ वा गहिवरल्या वनदेवींचा। सहदुःख भर साचा। गे हा हाय हंबरडा फोडी ।।१।। Translation: My silent grief, alas, Bursts forth in lamentation! (Chorus) Or the full measure of shared sorrow Of the grieving forest deities, alas, Bursts forth in lamentation!

(The war-horn sounds. Shakya soldiers enter, crying, "Enemy raid, arise!")

Shakya Sainik: Raid! Raid! General, the enemy's valiant general, Chanda, has launched a fearsome raid on our camp from the north! We were to launch our final assault on the enemy tomorrow, but as the enemy has suddenly attacked us beforehand, Vikramasimha, the Supreme Commander, considering this night the chance for a decisive conclusion, has himself engaged in the final battle. It is his command that all should proceed thither, fighting and striking.

Vallabha: Most reverently do I accept! Here is my sword raised! Arise, Sulochana, the national enemy has advanced—this is the final battle! Arise! For the welfare of the people, even the joy of personal demise must for a moment be set aside, just as the joy of personal life.

(Again, an uproar. "Help! Draw your weapons—help!")

Vallabha: Yes, I come! Nalini, I go! Till I return, wounded in this battle, to die beside her, protect the lifeless body of my beloved. If I do not return, then offer it, along with this camp, to the god of fire! And now, as I go, my friend, this is your lover's last, silent farewell.

Song:

Song Details: Title: Your beloved departs Tāla: | Chāl: Utho Piya Jago Original: सखा तुझा जातो । निरोपा सखि देई ।। ध्रु.।। जाण्यासी ज्या परत न येणे । त्या जाण्याच्या । निरोपा सखि देई ।। १।। आसूंत पुसल्या । उमटे न कंठी । मुका कामुक हा । निरोपा । सखि देई ।। २ ।। Translation: Your beloved departs, Give him farewell, my friend. (Chorus) For a departure whence there is no return, For that going, give him farewell, my friend. Wiped away by tears, it rises not in his throat, This silent lover's farewell, give it, my friend.

(He kisses her. "Come, sound the war-horn!" He exits with the soldiers.)

Sulochana: (Waking with a start) What! These war-horns! (Fumbling with her hands) Vallabha—awaken me—give me your hand— (Starts up) What? Has Vallabha gone? Or had he never come? Or was it all a dream?

Nalini: What is this, a rebirth? My friend, come, let me first embrace thee tightly! Devi, be not confused. Vallabha truly did come. But, unable to bear the excess of that sudden joy, you fell into a swoon and lay so insensible that we began to lament, thinking you had departed from us forever, when suddenly, to the north, a fierce assault was launched upon our army by the enemy! A great tumult of battle rages there. Thereupon, Vallabha plunged into it.

Sulochana: And left me thus? Did he deceive me when I asked him to awaken me for battle?

Nalini: What would they know that people rise from death for battle?

Sulochana: He knew! I had made such a pact with Death, even as I stepped into the doorway of its swoon, that Death should grant me a momentary respite just for this final battle, and allow me to fulfill my desire to share a couch with my Vallabha, even upon the battle-bed.

Nalini: Hark, has that tumultuous wave of battle penetrated your camp?

Sulochana: Why do you merely look? Let me draw this sword and leap into it!

Nalini: But you are weary from your swoon—

Sulochana: Has it not yet dawned upon you? Not weary from swoon. I am dead by death. But have you not heard that even after their heads are severed, brave warriors' headless torsos fight? Nalini, so shall this my headless torso fight, taking revenge for the Shakyas, striking off the heads of the enemy, hewing and striking, it shall go wherever Vallabha may be.

Nalini: Then change this woman's attire. Again into the former male disguise—

Sulochana: Nay, the masquerade of that guise is ended. That guise fought; now I, myself, shall fight! Bhavani (goddess of war) fought in woman's attire. A brave woman's valour surges tenfold in battle in woman's attire. I shall fight in woman's attire.

Song:

Song Details: Title: As Mahishasura-Mardini in battle Tāla: | Chāl: Bolo Bolo Bolo Original: महिषासुरमर्दिनी रणी जैशी ।। ध्रु.।। मुक्त- खड्ग- कर ऐशी ऐशी। स्त्रीवेषातचि लढे भवानी । वीरसुता मी नीरवल्लभा ।। दुष्ट दैत्य दल वधिनचि तैशी ।। १ ।। Translation: As Mahishasura-Mardini (Slayer of Mahishasura) in battle, With sword unsheathed in hand, thus, thus, Bhavani fought in woman's attire. (Chorus) I, daughter of heroes, bereft of my beloved, Shall similarly slay the host of wicked demons!

Nalini: Be watchful, my friend! The enemy!

(At that moment, Kosala soldiers enter, crying, "Victory to Kosala! Plunder, strike!")

All Soldiers: Strike! Kill!

One Soldier: But she is a woman.

Another Soldier: But she is a Shakya.

All Soldiers: Therefore, kill!

Sulochana: And she is a warrior, therefore kill!

(Battle ensues.)

All Soldiers: Victory to Kosala!

(They fight with roars.)

Sulochana and Nalini: Revenge for the Shakyas!

(They fight with roars.) (Some soldiers are killed, some retreat, and all exit, fighting.)

docs.title: Scene 6
docs.text:
(Chand, the Commander, enters from one side, and his followers from the other.)

Chand: What? Are these all the remaining soldiers of our army?

Anuchar: Aye; Kosala Commander Chand Mahashay (Sir), as per your command, these Kosala soldiers, who survived the battle on this dreadful night and were scattered across the battlefield, have been secretly gathered and brought forth. The enemy ranks have also been utterly decimated. The former Shakya general, Sulochan, was in fact Vallabha’s wife, Sulochana. This you have already learned. That woman—

Chand: Woman? In the ambush we laid this night, all the Shakyas indeed fought with utmost valour; but if anyone truly displayed prowess among them all, it was that woman! In male attire, she fought like Death itself; then, reverting to a woman, like a witch! When, even in the darkness, I recognised and struck Vallabha with a mortal blow, I then saw her, wounded yet fighting fiercely, in the distant light. Later—

Anuchar: She must have fallen lifeless there. Among the entire Shakya army, only one Vikramsinh, though himself wounded, was seen roaming the battlefield with some followers, like a blood-lusty tiger, pursuing us with the torch of battle still aflame. The rest of the Shakya army has been cut down; Commander Chand! And our own—

Chand: The Shakyas fought with such unexpected valour today! Had they fought thus from the outset of the war, we would not have dared to invade them. Nevertheless, I have fulfilled the mission given by His Majesty. The last of the Shakya army has been annihilated. I believe I should take with me another invaluable prize, worthy of offering at the feet of His Majesty Vidudbha, even more than this victory, before proceeding thither. Mark this: if the very trace of the Shakya name is to be erased, then that Buddha must disappear. Be not startled, for even today, he could sow hatred against us in the hearts of thousands from other castes, for Kosala’s treachery against the Shakyas; indeed, he might already be doing so. Therefore, I had intended to slay him in this very ambush; my endeavour to achieve that purpose still does not release me.

Anuchar: But to escape from here with our lives is itself difficult.

Chand: If the Shakyas cease fighting, then we shall not transgress the word of Bhagavan (Lord) Buddha and shall make a treaty with the Shakyas; hence, we had previously sent him an alluring invitation for Buddha to come and dissuade the Shakyas from senseless violence. And Buddha, beguiled by this, had agreed to come here this very night. Before dawn, he is still likely to come along this path from the hill to that monastery yonder. Until then, let us lie in wait. If he does not come, we shall escape at daybreak. But if he comes, ah, then! I shall sever his head and crown this Shakya victory! Then, even if we remaining warriors perish in that cause, it matters not. His simple-minded and weak counsel, born of contempt for the force of arms, made the Shakyas simple-minded and proved useful to us. But now, it is expedient not to keep alive him who makes Kosala itself simple-minded. Come! Let us lie hidden by that path beyond these scattered corpses and mounds.

(They exit.)

Sulochana: (Entering, blood-stained, hair dishevelled) In this darkness, as far as my sight reaches, I have searched every corpse on this battlefield, but my Vallabha (Beloved), wounded and fallen, is yet nowhere to be seen. When my Nālini (personal name/endearment) perished in battle, from somewhere here rose the roaring challenge of that hero, that Vallabha of mine. My life! Thy task of avenging the Shakyas, as far as possible, is complete. Now it is true that I should let thee go. But my life, for a moment, just for a moment, hold on! Once I have applied the dust from the feet of my Vallabha, fallen on the field of battle, then I shall cast off this body and, my life, consider thee freed.

(Gazing at the corpses.) Vallabha, Vallabha! There remains no one human to ask for information! Ye gods, deities, spirits, ghosts, forest-deities, war-deities, ye who hear these human questions of my mind, tell me! Where lies the wounded body of the Shakya Commander, Virsinh Vallabha! Vallabha, we were to share the battle-bed together, were we not? Then where art thou alone; I have come to keep thee company, wait a moment, Vallabha! Vallabha—

Vallabha: (Rising slightly from the battlefield) What is this cry of Sulochana! She had reached the other shore of death, leaving me behind, had she not? Am I then so near to death that I can distinctly hear the call from death's other shore? How swiftly the boat of unconsciousness bears me across the Vaitaraṇī (mythological river of death)!

Sulochana: Vallabha, art thou anywhere here! Vallabha—

Vallabha: Oh, my beloved Sulochana! Is this truly thou?

Sulochana: (Running towards him) Yes, my dear, it is I, my Nath (Lord)! It is I, your Sulochana, who pursued you relentlessly! When you laid me down, dead from your lap, and departed alone for battle, I was so startled that I awoke even from death, and true to my vow, striking and wounding the enemy in your wake, I have returned to your feet. Companion of the bed of love, grant me a place on this battle-bed too, wilt thou not? This is my last plea—

Song:

Song Details: Title: Aṅganā ratiraṅgī Chāl: Abarit bhar āī Original: अंगना रतिरंगी । शेजारी रतिशेजेची । रण शेजेसहि घेई रणरंगी ।। ध्रु.।। जाग जीतुनी येणे नाही । गाढ झोप ती येते पाही । सरक जरा मज निजु दे संगी ।। १ ।। Translation: Oh, companion of love's sport, of love's soft bed, Receive me too upon this battle-bed, in battle dread. (Chorus) No waking will there be from this victorious sleep, A slumber profound, behold, doth o'er me creep. Move close, a space beside thee let me keep.

Sulochana: Look not at me; embrace me not one last time!

Vallabha: My life-breaths, draw forth the dwindling flame of my senses but once more. In its flicker, let me see my beloved, feel her, perceive her!

Sulochana: Ah, my love, how soft and enchanting this battle-bed feels, like that bed of love born of desire and duty!

Vallabha: For this reason, that bed of love, desirable though it was, was as auspicious and meritorious as this battle-bed of dharma (righteous duty).

Sulochana: By such a death, our lives have found fulfilment. Our story has reached a happy end.

Vallabha: Whether any event concludes happily or tragically depends upon what we consider happiness. To fight unto death for the welfare of the people was our wish yesterday; that it has been fulfilled, makes even death a happy end! Ah! Sulochana, art thou near? My life—this is the last call, Sulochana—

Sulochana: And this is the last, oh! Oh Vallabha!

(She collapses, her head upon his breast, just as Vikramsinh and soldiers enter with hilāl (crescent sword).)

Vikram: A sound came from somewhere here. Hmm, come this way, let us see! Ah, this is my brave son, the brave general of the Shakyas, Vallabha, and alas, alas! Nay, thrice blessed! This is my daughter-in-law, Vallabha’s Vallabhā, the war-deity (raṇadevată) of the Shakyas, Sulochana! Bravo, my child! When, in the carnage of this night’s battle, I learned that the young warrior Sulochan in this Shakya army was none other than my daughter-in-law, Sulochana, the joyful wonder I felt seeing thee fight like a descending lightning bolt is now doubled with delight and astonishment to behold thee here, like a lightning bolt held by some magic, embracing thy beloved even on the bed of death, lying lifeless! Oh, the devoted marital duty (naiṣṭhika kāmacharya) of these heroic lovers, male and female, is not one whit less in sanctity than the devoted celibacy (brahmacharya) of an ascetic; in beneficence, it may even be slightly more! That Devi Yashodhara is called a renunciant foremost female disciple (Agraśrāvikā), a great nun (Mahābhikṣuṇī) among the Shakyas, is fitting indeed. But the renunciation, self-control, and devotion to duty of this young maiden, Sulochana, this worshipper of Kāmadeva (god of love), are as intense as those of that great Devi Yashodhara, and her martyrdom (hutātmatā) is truly extraordinary! Oh, ye worshippers of Kāmadeva, what can be more selfless, detached, and unattached than such auspicious, desire-filled devotion to union as yours! My brave, virtuous, beautiful daughter-in-law, child Sulochana, this last embrace given to thy great hero Vallabha on the death-couch, this final desirable sacrament of Kāmadeva's worship for you both, is as auspicious as any religious rite of deity worship; it is holy; it is conducive to the welfare of all young maidens (kanyaka) and youths (kumāra).

Chand: (Crouching, peering forward with his soldiers) Naik (Leader), there are not so many men with this Vikram as you said. There are only as many as ourselves. And he is wounded, so what are you waiting for? Before the Buddha, crush the throat of this prey (mṛgayā), which has walked into our mouths, with your teeth like a hawk!

(Shouting, "Victory to King of Kosala! (Kośaleśvar Mahārāj kī Jay!)" they fall upon Vikram.) O oath-breaker (vratabhraṣṭa) Vikram, I was searching for thee! Take this!

(He strikes.)

Vikram: O wicked Chand, I too was searching for thee! Take this!

(He strikes.)

Buddha Disciple: (Entering with the Buddha) Ha! Ha! Tathāgata Bhagavān Buddha (The Enlightened, Blessed Buddha) counsels both of you to be calm. For he has come to establish peace.

Chand: Away! Wouldst thou snatch a deer from a lion's mouth?

(He rushes at Vikram.)

Buddha: (Supporting Vikram) Vikram, Commander Chand is battle-crazed (raṇonmat). Anger, like an enraged serpent, becomes uncontrollable for anyone. But you are wise. You know our religious aphorism (dharma sūtra): ‘Akrōdhēna jiyēt krōdham | Asādhum sādhunā jiyēt |’ (Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the evil with good.)

Chand: What, vile Buddha, dost thou call me evil (asādhu)? Dost thou call the Kosala Commander evil? I shall cut off thy tongue, take this!

(He advances upon the Buddha.)

Vikram: (Striking Chand and wounding him, then felling him and planting his foot on his chest) Bhagavān, has his anger been appeased by your non-anger at least? Or has he, conversely, grown more frenzied? If this sword, protector of the good (sādhuparitravāṇa), had not intervened, the righteous Buddha would now have been slain by the wicked (duṣṭa) Chand.

Buddha: But whatever has happened, such killing does not become you; you are an ascetic (saṁnyāsī)!

Vikram: And precisely for that reason, the first and most fatal blow to sever the head of this incorrigible public menace (loka kaṇṭak) must be struck by this very renounced sword of mine! It has been struck; I have finally slain this villain (chaṇḍāḷa) myself. This body of mine, weakened by wounds from battle, will fall in half a moment. But it will fall now with even greater fulfilment! Ah! By the spurting splashes of his blood, my ascetic garb and this renounced sword of mine—

Buddha: Have been stained by a sinful blackness (kāḷibhyāne) that can never be washed away.

Vikram: Bhagavān, come into the light of reality and look closely, for any with eyes can tell that this is a brilliant red colour, not black. Stained by the red blood of that wicked man, the original sickly, pale yellow of this ascetic's demeanour has vanished, and it appears vibrant, crimson, and radiant like the rising sun! In forty years of unarmed asceticism (niḥśastra saṁnyāsa), I could not accumulate as much beneficence (paropakāra) and merit (puṇya) as I have gathered in this single moment by wielding this ascetic’s weapon, granting life to countless innocent souls. If readiness for public welfare is the worldly duty of an ascetic, then I have never performed it with such intensity as I have today. Therefore, today I truly appear as an ascetic and a monk.

Buddha: O Mahāmanā (Great-souled one) Vikram, though your logical argument (koṭikram) may seem unassailable from the perspective of worldly gains and losses (aihik lābhālābh), from an otherworldly (pāralaukik) standpoint, you have deviated today from the great vow (mahāvrata) of non-violence (ahiṁsā), in accordance with the ascetic's dharma, which you had taken. Thereby, a desireless (vitṛṣṇa), supremely wise (param jñānī), and foremost renunciant monk (tyāgī bhikṣu pravar) like you, though very near to Nirvāṇa (liberation/enlightenment), has today fallen from Nirvāṇa (Nirvāṇachyut).

Vikram: If I am denied the state of Nirvāṇa for this fault of slaying this wicked man to avert the violence against countless innocent men and women that would ensue from Chand’s tyranny, then I condemn (dhikkār) such Nirvāṇa. That which is obtained only by aiding the oppression of millions of people is not Nirvāṇa but hell (naraka).

Dharma: (Manifesting) But O great practitioner of Karma Yoga (Mahākarmayogin), hero, you have not fallen from Nirvāṇa. On the contrary, by this very martyrdom, you have attained the state of Nirvāṇa. For,

Dvāvimau puruṣau loke Sūryamaṇḍalabhedinau | Parivrāṭ yogayuktaścha raṇe chābhimukhe hataḥ || (Two kinds of men in this world pierce the solar orb: The wandering ascetic (parivrāṭ) devoted to Yoga, And he who is slain in battle, facing forward.)

Vikram: O divine being, who art thou? A god or an angel (Devdūta)?

Dharma: I am Dharma, the foundation (dharmādhishṭhān) of all human righteousness. O Buddha-deva, you are supreme among wandering ascetics! Humanity (mānuṣakāvar) owes you infinite gratitude. This Shakya nation and this Shakya race have perished today, but they passed away after fulfilling their chief life’s work. For they gave birth to Tathāgata Buddha! And therefore, in a sense, they are immortal. Gods and demons, yakṣas (nature spirits) and takṣakas (serpent-demons), Āryas (noble ones) and Anāryas (non-noble ones), all of humanity, from islands to continents, shall seek out this your birthplace as the most sacred land, to offer their floral oblations of devotion (bhaktibhāvāchyā puṣpāñjali) here. The histories of this Shakya race shall be studied like religious epics (dharmapurāṇā sārakhe); kings and emperors shall cast their crowns, and the seven seas their rubies and pearls, before your image. Millions upon millions of human heads, which have not bowed before any man’s feet, shall humbly bow before the feet of your meditative image for ages to come. O wandering ascetic, great karma-renunciant Buddha, you are indeed worthy of the state of Nirvāṇa; but O hero, great practitioner of Karma Yoga Vikram, you too are worthy of that same state of Nirvāṇa! For, to achieve the ultimate good of humanity, which is the chief essence of Dharma, you renounced everything and fought for public welfare (lokakalyāṇārth) in direct combat, slaying those who harm the people! You did not even flinch from sacrificing your own life (prāṇatyāg). Unfortunately, your memory as an individual will not endure like the Buddha’s. But fame is often a matter of chance; it is not the sole indicator of merit. And the terrible penalty that this Shakya race has had to pay for this oblivion of your Karma Yoga’s greatness, how this feeble Shakya nation fell prey to the violence of powerful villains due to its neglect of armed strength and the extreme asceticism of agriculture, women, and the sword (kṛṣi, kāminī, kṛpāṇ), so too, and for almost the same reasons, will this entire Āryāvarta (ancient India) fall prey to the demonic invasions of Yavanas, Huns, and Shakas (yavana-huṇa-śakāṁchyā rākṣasī ākramaṇāsa). This destruction of the Shakya nation today is merely a premonition of the grave danger that will befall the entire Āryāvarta in the future. It is merely a preliminary experiment conducted by Time on a small scale. Hero Vikram, adopting the auspicious, power-worshipping Karma Yoga (śubha kāmī śaktipūjak karmayoga) that you preached and practiced, which contains all the worldly and otherworldly benefits of inactive asceticism yet is supremely beneficial for the people, is the means to liberation from the clutches of that danger. Since the true nature and objective of Dharma, which is the worldly and otherworldly sustenance and salvation of humanity, is achieved to a greater extent through such Karma Yoga, O humanity, my definite and best opinion is that although—

Saṁnyāsaḥ karmayogaścha niḥśreyasakārāvubhau || Tathāpi -- tayostu karmasaṁnyāsāt karmayogo viśiṣyate || (Renunciation and the path of action both lead to supreme good. Yet, of the two, the path of action is superior to the renunciation of action.)

[End of Play]
